## Decision: We are going to protect the abovementioned endpoints using the following approach:
 
1. We will increment a counter in our persistent store (Redis) with every failed attempt.
2. The counter will be rate limited per actor, by means of a time-to-live.
3. Once the counter reaches a pre-defined threshold, the actor will be locked out for a period defined by an exponential algorithm.
4. During a period of exponential lockout, all authentication attempts will be responded with a 403 Forbidden. The exponential algorithm should allow for sufficient time to prevent brute force attacks, but also allow genuine users to retry without undue delay.
 5. If the exponential algorithm extends past a certain pre-defined time (e.g. 24 hours), the actor will be permanently locked out and directed to contact the OPG for assistance.
 6. Failed counter, exponential lockouts and permalockouts will all be persisted, and made visible to the OPG support teams.

## Decision: To replace the term 'environment' with three new concepts:

### Location

This represents an **Azure subscription** which acts as a logical container for all infrastructure and applications required to run a specific environment within. We should aim to have only one Location per subscription for consistency.

A location is the highest level of resource segregation we can achieve within an infrastructure code module. We are only allowed to create one set of CNP infrastructure per subscription.

Within a Location a resource group will be created for each environment, providing a location-level resource segregation between environments.

### Environment

A collection of applications, databases and other infrastructure components required to run a version of the CNP applications. Each Environment will have a uniquely addressable endpoint for UI, API Gateway, etc. Environments are run from a Location.

An Environment is a single runtime of the full CNP system within a given Location. The applications on this environment will share infrastructure and the same database.

### Instance

A single service/component that belongs to a specific environment. Multiple instances may exist on the same environment. For example: `ccd-data-store` has 2 instances, one instance for `ccd-admin-web` and another instance for `ccd-data-store-api`.

An instance is a single running application/microservice of the full CNP System within an environment.

## Decision: This ADR has to be implemented in many different phases.

Phase 1:
- The integration frontend translations (`strings.json`) need to be split into 3 files:
    - `strings.json` for config flows, but no longer for titles
    - `options.json` for option flows
    - `automations.json` for device automations (no more merging of device automations between integrations)
    - the existing `strings.sensor.json` is moved to `state.json` and kept for backwards compatibility. Note: if the integration had its `strings.json` split up, its `state.json` needs to also be split up into 3 files.

Phase 2:
- Drop `title` key from integrations frontend strings. Instead, the translations of `title` will be part of the `strings.json` or `config.json` translation files. 
- The translation server/client side should be updated such that `config_entry.get_translations_for_domain(domain)` will return the integration name and config flow strings.
- Drop `strings.sensor.json`
- Remove state from `strings.json` of integrations that do use state. This is only done for moon and season (see Context).

Phase 3:
- Add a new API to fetch frontend translations. It takes optional parameter `domain`, an optional parameter `integration_domains` and optional parameter `components`.
    - If `domain` is passed, the integration translations will be loaded (excluding integrations for component `components`).
    - If `integration_domains` is passed (always needs to be an array of string), the integration translations will be loaded for all those domains (excluding integrations for component `components`).
    - If `components` is passed, all frontend translations of any integration under the component `components` will be returned. Note: `integration_domains` overrides `components` except when they don't share any integration and except when `integration_domains` is empty. The `components` array has to be an array of string.
    - If nothing is passed, it will return the same as what the current API does.
    - `state` will be loaded in all cases.
- Add new API to fetch frontend translations for state. It takes optional parameter `domain`.
- The new frontend API will be split from the `frontend` component. It will have no components. The configuration will be integrated in `http`.
- The `frontend` component no longer supports `title` and will no longer handle translations.

Phase 4: Remove `config` component. All frontend translations will be part of our translation server. All relevant integration names will be part of the translation server.
The config flow info used for integrations will come from `integrations.json` and so will include the name of the integration.

```text

##Decision: Given that we have already chosen to use ActiveRecord as our ORM, we believe ActiveStorage will give us all of
the functionality we need to implement our file storage feature, while being the most straightforward option to
implement. There is no functionality in Shrine we believe we will need, while the benefits it provides to more complicated
systems don't apply to our usecase at the moment. ActiveStorage is also the standard solution for a Rails application,
which will make it easier for future developers to understand our implementation.
 
Note, that there is one known issue with ActiveStorage's generic `ActiveStorage::Attachment` in that it increases
complexity when querying by the filename attribute. In this case, there are only two associations to traverse, which
is manageable, and we do not expect to be doing much querying by filename, so we don't anticipate issues. We expect
ActiveStorage will continue to evolve and become a more mature solution over the lifetime of the project, so that by the
time we need to perform these more complicated operations we expect the gem will have evolved to better support them.

Finally, we also explored a solution that is completely removed from Rails, such as uploading directly to AWS S3.
AWS offers its own Javascript SDK and Ruby SDKs to handle file uploads. With this solution, the process would be to
generate a signed url via the backend, and use this on the frontend to upload a file directly to AWS. Once complete,
the frontend would notify the backend of the file url, and a record would be created. While this option would give
us the most flexibility and control, the initial implementation would take the longest amount of time, and in our
context we do not expect to have a large number of images, or large images uploaded in parallel. For these reasons
we decided against this option, opting instead to use a well tested and feature complete gem to avoid spending
development time and increasing our risk.

## Decision: We'll use a [JWT token](https://jwt.io) to transmit the information
needed to authenticate our users with Marsha.

A JWT token (JSON Web Token) is a standard [RFC 7519](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7519)
defining a compact and self-contained way for securely transmitting
information between parties as a JSON object.

We have a custom validator for JWTs. All JWTs will pass through it.

Marsha has no internal mechanism to create the JWT. The decision to
use such a token does not define an internal process that uses or
stores user identities. User identities don't even need to be stored
in Marsha and are not tied to some external user system that may
change at some point.

The Marsha JWT contains some claims:

### General Claims

* `aud`: audience. Who the JWT is intended for. Should always be
  `marsha.lms.app`
* `exp`: expiration time. After this time the JWT will be refused
* `iat`: issued-at time. For information only.
* `iss`: issuer. The URL of the consumer site that created the JWT.
  Needed to know what shared-secret to use for verifying the JWT signature.
* `jti`: JWT unique ID.
* `locale`: The 2-letters language code (ISO 639-1) of the consumer site.
* `oauth`: OAuth information. Required only if you're using OIDC and you want
  to pass it to LTI provider through Marsha.
* `roles`: A list of strings. Each string define a role granted to
  the user to interact with the objects identified in the other claims.
* `session_id`: This defines the ID of a session. It could be for example
  the session ID of an LMS or of another platform using Marsha. If provided, Marsha
  will ignore `permissions.set_default_permissions` and save permissions with
  the session ID instead of having 2 entries in `ResourceAccess` table with the same
  object ID and user ID but different permissions set.
  This allows to have the same user and object with different access for different
  sessions and to handle for example different accesses of the same user for
  different classrooms in Moodle. If `session_id` is missing, Marsha will fall back
  to the classic behaviour where `permissions.set_default_permissions` is
  used and there's 1 unique entry for 1 unique user and object.
* `user`: An object identifying the user and giving information about the user.
* `resource`: An object containing the data identifying the resource concerned by the JWT
  and information on this resource. This resource is
  generally a [LTI consumer context](https://www.imsglobal.org/spec/lti/v1p3/tool.html#lti-context-claim).

### Consumer Site

The consumer site is the website or platform hosting videos (LMS, CMS...)
with Marsha. Each consumer site can have a shared secret which is
a `UUID` and allows Marsha to trust a JWT signed by this consumer site.
Marsha won't trust any JWT that's not signed by a registered
consumer site.

The JWT contains the URL of the consumer site:
`eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJodHRwczovL21vb2RsZS5sZXR2aWRlby5jb20ifQ...`
The URL is then used to find the shared secret in Marsha. This shared
secret is used to verify the JWT signature.

### Permissions

The JWT also contains an object defining a set of permissions for the user
in question. This object defines a user and resource
id pairing along with granted permissions.

```json
  "permissions": {
    "can_access_dashboard": false,
    "can_update": true,
    "can_read": true,
    "can_share": true,
    "set_default_permissions": {
      "student": [
        "set_read",
        "set_token"
      ],
      "annotator": [
        "set_read",
        "set_token"
      ],
      "instructor": [
        "set_read",
        "set_update",
        "set_token",
        "set_playlist_user"
      ]
    },
    "set_permissions_with_object_id": {
      "22222

## Decision: We propose to replace email based root access as defined above with role based root access via the control account. To support the existing setup, and in order to allow a migration time frame, the control account also sets up root email addresses, but doesn't hand them out to team members directly.

The root email address is composed using the following syntax:

`root@<ACCOUNTNAME>.<ORGPREFIX>.rootmail.<REGION>.superwerker.cloud`

The control account is used as the AWS account handling inbound mail for all other accounts within the control account VPC using the SES mail receiving capabilities.

The SES action `StopAction` is used to prevent the mailbox from receiving mails from outside sources.

The SES action `S3Action` is used to store root mails in an S3 bucket that can only be written to by SES within the control account, read only by members of the admin group of the control account.

The SES action `LambdaAction` is used to handle mails by sending them to Slack for notifications.

To provide privileged access to read the root emails, the control account uses a read-only cross-account role with a read-only policy to the S3 bucket that is only assumable by the root role.

The root user is also configured using the following policies:

- The `AdministratorAccess` policy for convenience (and to allow for manual setup and cleanup of resources when needed)
- An identity-based policy allowing to create a new access key

## Decision: We are going to go with an **actor based architecture** to decouple the different functional pieces of the Holochain node. An example actor, an abstraction of an agent component with its own local state that runs concurrently, are the network, state, etc. We will use the [tokio](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio) framework to enable this concurrency.

Within an agent, each actor can only communicate via explicit messages to one another in an asynchronous way. An agent can choose to reply with a reply message or not.

Actors interact by sending `HdkAction` to one another. Each `HdkAction` contains a `trace_id` field to trace each interaction between different actors which we can then use for logging/debugging purposes. Every `HdkAction` is replied with a `HdkAgentResult`.

We are also going to use [Redux](https://redux.js.org/) (a pattern derived from the [Elm](https://elm-lang.org/) architecture to enable the management of the whole agent’s state within one single data structure.

The overall model of the agent’s loop will be the following:

- the **reducer**: a pure function that takes the previous `state` and the `action` and returns the next `state`. (Each actor will have its own individual reducer).

- the **action**: a plain object that contains information about changes to the state. The **action** must have a `type` property. (An actor can choose to ignore an **action** if the `type` property is not in line with what that actor expects).

- the **store**: an object that brings together the reducer, action and state.

We will use the [`dux`](https://github.com/mafintosh/dux) (a tiny redux alternative) to integrate the agent state management into the actor based architecture. Every actor will interact with its individual `store` instead of with the monolithic Redux store and the `store` will take care of bringing all of them together.

## Decision: It was decided to refactor our event processing from Callback based to Channel
based, using a bounded channel which is created for every new request between a
`Handle` and the main `Supervisor` to transport the `Supervisor` response back
to the `Handle`.

This leads to the removal of `Callback` and `CallbackEvent` as well as the
removal of async `Handle` methods.
Additionally the `Context` is now created for every new `Worker` that is spawned
and carries the `Handle` of the `Supervisor` to allow every spawned `Worker` to
communicate directly to the `Supervisor`.
The `Context` also carries a reference to the `Supervisor` `Sender` that can be
used to issue a request and await its response.
The `Sender` is used to create a new `Channel` for every new request the user
spawns and issues that to `Supervisor` to be passed on.
All request initiated by a new `Worker` are done on the newly created
`Context` of the `Worker` and have a `timeout_ms` of 5000 milliseconds to avoid
indefinite request loops.

When a message is received by a `Worker` that is not a `Supervisor` request a
`Context` is also generated for it. That is then passed to the worker receive
method alongside the original message to allow the `Worker` to initiate new
requests with the `Supervisor` and retrieve the responses on the new context as
the result of the receive method.

In order to avoid issues due to race conditions during a channel based
refactoring the new request event and Supervisor is behind a `feature =
"channel_based_refactor"` compilation flag which allows to continue work on the
channel based solution as it will be completely backward compatible.

## Decision: - Patients receive text notifications via SMS, WhatsApp (India), or Imo (Bangladesh).
- SMS will provide basic information (eg. you missed a check-up).
- Whatsapp and Imo will provide a more interactive experience, which could include the patient reporting their blood pressure, a link to speak with a physician, or links to educational videos.
- Both SMS and Whatsapp will link back to a health.care web portal for additional information.
- SMS is implemented using an Twilio API in `care/utils.py`.
- Whatsapp and Imo are implemented using a third-party notification service, Gupshup, with an API in `care/utils.py`.
- SMS notifications for Bangladesh is turned on in the [config file](https://github.com/coronasafe/care_fe/blob/staging/src/config.js). Whatsapp and Imo can be turned on in the same place.

The overall architecture looks like this:

![notifications architecture](./whatsapp-imo-notifications-architecture.png)

This architecture separates patient notifications from the Care patient database. This is a common strategy when dealing with medical information, and it is also the [HIPAA-compliant way](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/communication-services/concepts/hippa-compliance) to use the Twilio and Gupshup services. The patient notification database has a 1-1 relationship with the patient ID in the Care patient database, but it contains absolutely no health or Personally Identifiable Information beyond the patient ID and contact information.

To accomplish this, we'll create a new patient notification database that stores the patient contact number and any channel-specific authentication information (eg. Gupshup user ID). A new microservice will then listen to changes in the patient notification database and use the Twilio and Gupshup APIs to send notifications as needed.

Additionally, to deal with notification timeouts and errors, there will be two separate tables in the notification database, one that stores pending notifications, and one that stores completed notifications. The microservice will have two separate cron jobs. One cron job will move pending notifications with a timeout from the pending table to the complete table with a timeout message. The second cron job will attempt to send pending notifications, moving them to the complete table when successful or with an error message when unsuccessful.

## Decision: We reviewed the proposal here
[https://github.com/dapr/dapr/issues/849](https://github.com/dapr/dapr/issues/849)

The proposal covers two important scenarios:
1. Versioning as it relates to HTTP App Callbacks: In this case, each call to the App needs to carry the API version in a form that the app is aware of so that it can return an appropriate response. The format and mechanism of doing this is in the proposal itself.
2. The DAPR Runtime and its interaction with the App.
This is important because today if we were to take the existing version of DAPR (say v0.3) and have it try to interact with an App that implements v0.4, it would break. Even if the DAPR runtime had logic to know that app implements a specific API version, it would fail to interact with it properly. We need to decide what would be the best behavior for the DAPR Runtime in this situation.

We agreed that for the runtime the best solution is to follow semantic versioning. 
- In the case of a new App Callback API version, e.g. v1.x (a patch version based on semantic versioning) which adds to an existing API contract, the behavior for a DAPR runtime that does not understand that version will be that of ignoring any new API’s that it does not know of. Existing API calls will continue to work normally and will be dispatched to the App.
- In the case of a new App Callback API version, e.g. v2.x (a major version based on semantic versioning) which removes an existing API contract, or fundamentally alters an existing contract such that the runtime cannot understand or correctly interact with it, a DAPR runtime that does not understand that version should fail at startup.

## Decision: When an item is marked as deleted in `itemRecords`, its ID will be appended to
the `deletedItemIds` entry in the item metadata in the preserving service's
namespace:

```
metadata.preservingService.deletedItemIds = [
  ...metadata.preservingService.deletedItemIds,
  id
]
```

This ensures that the `deletedItemIds` entries are always unique.

These entries will be appended *after* the `itemRecords.deleted` flag has been
set to true to prevent a situation in which a preserving service can restore
an item which the database considers deleted but not all traces of which have
actually been deleted.

When an item is restored by a preserving service, its ID should be removed
from the `deletedItemIds` list before the `itemRecords.deleted` flag is set
to false. The following code will implement this operation:

```
metadata.preservingService.deletedItemIds = metadata.preservingService.deletedItemIds
  .filter((currentId) => currentId !== id)
```

The preservation service is responsible for updating the `deletedItemIds` in the
`items` collection to match the state of `deletedItemIds` in `metadata`. The service
is also responsible for performing the filter operation described above, since it is
the only code that knows what `id` is.

This decision also creates the implicit decision of storing item metadata by
preservation service ID, which will be implemented in a separate but immediately
consecutive task.

### Why not restore by ID?

`PUT /items/:id/restore` is currently only an endpoint provided by our own preservation
microservice, not by any of the services which we preserve items from. Therefore, since
the other services are responsible for the restoration of items, they must also be
responsible for finding items to restore.

## Decision: We are going to make our decisions, and record them in an Architecture Decision Record (ADR), as inspired by Michael Nygard (of [_Release It!_](http://www.informit.com/store/release-it!-design-and-deploy-production-ready-software-9780978739218) fame) and his post on [_Documenting Architecture Decisions_](http://thinkrelevance.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions).

An ADR is a short, simple text file that documents a single decision. We can version-control the ADR, along with our other technical documentation, in an ADR repo.

## Decision: We will use the approach of Architecture Decisions Records, as described by M. Nygard.

For each architectural decision, we will write a file (in Markdown) structured as following :

```
{date of change}-A short sentence to explain what change is made (the change name must be unique).
  
A short sentence or two to summarize what the decision is.

Optional: A list of technologies/libraries/frameworks used for this change
* [ ] Technology A
* [ ] Technology B
* [ ] Technology C

### Context

A paragraph (or two) to explain what problem is to solve, what are the use cases, etc.

You can also list here all the possible options that could be chosen to make that change, with 
their pros and cons :
1. Option A (Pros: ..., Cons: ...)
2. Option B (Pros: ..., Cons: ...)

### Decision

One or two paragraphs that explains why we made that choice, and how it addresses all the 
problems listed in the "Context" section.

### Consequences

A paragraph to explain the consequences of this decision on the current and/or future of the project.

Optional: You can list a few use cases with an example code.

### Links

List of documents used for this decision.

### License

Your license
```

The version control will be used to track the changes in these records.

## Decision: We should measure the following three forms of uptime.

### Backend Uptime

We should measure the uptime of the backend service directly via automated polling from an external source.
This polling should check whether the API can be accessed without error.
It should be carried out from at least 3 geographically separated servers.
We want to measure downtime due to outages on the backend, not due to network problems.
This can be achieved by using a polling service that takes the majority of the poll results (at least 2 in this case) as ground truth.
If at least two polling servers say a server is down then we should take that to mean that it is actually down.

###Frontend Uptime

We should measure the uptime of the frontend service via automated polling from an external source.
This polling should check whether the frontend returns HTTP status 200 without error when accessed from a browser.
It should be carried out from at least 3 geographically separated servers.
As with the backend, we want to measure downtime due to outages, not due to network problems, and the same mechanism for achieving this applies to the frontend as well.

We could consider testing a frontend which actually has to call a backend, but then the frontend uptime measurement would become intertwined with the backend uptime measurement, and we want to keep them separate.
We want to distinguish between an outage that only affects the frontend from an outage which only affects the backend.

### End-to-end Uptime

We should measure uptime via automated polling from an external source that actually carries out an end-to-end user-level interaction.
It should test that a user could log in and carry out some basic action.
The action should be one which we would be embarrassed to be reported on social media as unavailable.
It is important to test real user journeys because these can fail when all the backend and frontend components are individually available.

## Context: We're using [Go](https://go.dev/) as our backend programming language.
Some libraries like the [Open Census Go Library](https://opencensus.io/go/) expect a [`context.Context`](https://pkg.go.dev/context) as an argument.
We also expect a `context.Context` from the HTTP request handler so that the request can be cancelled.
Therefore, we will have a `context.Context` to pass down the call stack.

However, since there is a `context.Context` already, we also have to consider passing down other parameters as the `context.Context`.
For example, we might want to pass down the user that makes an HTTP request for logging purposes.
The context can have key-value pairs stored in them.
We could potentially use the context as a dictionary of various parameters.

## Decision: We will store parameters in the `context.Context` in the following scenarios.

1. The parameter is a request-scoped metadata for logging, authentication or anything that doesn't define the behaviour of the call.
2. The parameter is a request-scoped dependency that is not provided by the [Dependency Injection Framework](DependencyInjection.md).
3. The parameter is a request-scoped state object that cannot be represented as return values. For example, a transaction object could be a request-scoped state object.
4. The parameter is provided by an external library.

When the parameters are stored in the context, we should pass them as pointers so that the parameters can be modified in the call chain.
We will have a common list of context key-value pairs.
For example:

| Key                                  | Value                   | Description                                                |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `contextKeyUser`                     | `*user`                 | User making the request                                    |
| `contextKeyToken`                    | `*token`                | Token for the request for authentication                   |
| `contextKeyDBTransaction`            | `*sql.Tx`               | Database transaction of the request                        |

We will have a common list of utility functions for reading and writing these to the `context.Context`.
For example:

```go
func UserFromContext(ctx context.Context) *User {
	v := ctx.Value(contextKeyUser)
	if v == nil {
		return nil
	}
	return v.(*User)
}

func UserToContext(ctx context.Context, u *User) context.Context {
	return context.WithValue(ctx, contextKeyUser, u)
}
```

This decision would have to be revisited if we were to use another concurrency primitive other than `context.Context` or if we decide to change the logging strategy.

## Decision: We are going to build a data pipeline using a combination of the following technologies: - AWS DMS (Database Migration Service) and Kinesis Data Streams for data ingestion - AWS Kinesis Data Firehose for easy S3 and Redshift streaming and retention - AWS S3 for long-term storage - AWS Glue for running transformation jobs to clean and add contextual data to the ingested data - AWS Redshift for storing transformed and report-specific data - AWS QuickSight for building dashboard reports using data in Redshift
### Pros - AWS DMS is very stable, has a low cost, and very few operational concerns, especially when using CDC on top of Kinesis Data Streams - S3 is very low-cost and stable - Redshift gives us SQL-based analytics for reporting and scales well - QuickSight gives us easy dashboarding over Redshift - Overall the approach gives us the ability to easily ingest data from multiple datasources into a data lake to use for both reports and later for model training - The data is separated from the main production database, which means we can experiment on it without fear of impacting the production application. It also provides a backup/snapshot of production data that is separated from the production database - Overall cost for the pipeline seems to be about $300 a month - Can be very extensible and gives us a great platform for building future reports and ML projects - We can have a lot of control and visibility of the data we're ingesting and transforming ### Cons - Has a fairly steep learning curve and a fairly complex set of technologies to work with, especially when adding Kinesis - May have fairly long iteration cycles for building new reports and dashboards
### Implementation Details ### AWS Kinesis In order to simplify the DMS ingestion part, we will follow the AWS suggested [CDC architecture diagram](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/CHAP_Task.CDC.html) using Kinesis Data Streams. ![dms architecture diagram](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/images/cdc-architecture.png) This will work as follows: 1. DMS will use our [replica](https://simpledotorg.atlassian.net/browse/SERVER-250) to ingest all the initial data from our production database. This will prevent any impact on the production database and should happen fairly quickly 2. Once the initial data is complete, DMS will be switched to CDC mode and read the replica's WAL (write ahead logs) in real-time and send it to our Kinesis Data Stream 3. The Kinesis Data Stream will batch the data and send it to our Kinesis Data Firehose 4. The Firehose will write the batched data to both S3 and Redshift and will be available for ETL via AWS Glue 5. Our ETL jobs in Glue will be triggered on a time-based schedule
### AWS Redshift We will be using Amazon Redshift to power our reports and for most of our data aggregation. We will try to implement [CDC on top of Redshift](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/CHAP_Task.CDC.html) by taking advantage of the `UPDATE_FLAG` and `LSN` fields we will be getting in the Kinesis Data Streams when the Firehose populates Redshift. Our ETL job would then aggregate the latest changes from the CDC events and update the data in our Redshift tables on a time-based schedule. This will allow us to easily report on the most up-to-date data.

## Decision: ### Decision regarding error echoing

The initial proposal was to disable error echoing by default. We have reconsidered this decision because:

- Command echoing is often desired to add context to a step's output. Errors provide additional context as to what went wrong and are an important part of the step's log.
- Many commands can output to stdout without error (e.g. `ls -R /does/not/exist`). Disabling error echoing means these errors are suppressed completely in user logs.
- There are no simple ways to disable this behaviour if the user so chooses.

For these reasons, command echoing will still be enabled in the case there is an error in processing the command. This will be the default behavior and is not able to be disabled.

### Decision regarding echoing for other cases

Echoing is disabled for the following scenarios by default. This behaviour can be explicitly toggled by using the `::echo::on` and `::echo::off` commands:

- If `ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG` secret is not enabled
- When using script bodies

Otherwise echoing is enabled by default for:

- Explicit `run` commands
- Pre/main/post steps

## Decision: * The notion of input as tuples is replaced by the notion of input
as vectors. Tuples can still be thought of as a special case for the
`[u64, &str, Value]` tuple type used to input data into the DB
arrangement.

* The notion of input as a single source is replaced by the notion of
input as collections, or arrangements. We introduce two generic
interfaces, `Source` and `Arranger`, respectively, to define how these
two interfaces can be used to load data from external sources and to
materialize arrangements from collections.

* Sources can be linked to arrangements by means of a `Link` type
that combines the generic `Source` and `Arranger` into an interface
where one can simply invoke `poll` to trigger the reading of data from
the source and the insertion into the arrangement.

* All links have a time component, which represents the time the data
was read from the external source. As such, the notion of DB time
(the time a fact was recorded by a Datomic transaction) is replaced
by the notion of source time. As we expect that different sources have
different latencies, and we wish to support sources with an internal
time axis, this requires an additional time mapping. Therefore we also
introduce the notion of an input time that maps from the source time
to the DB time using a function `f(x)` for each input collection `i`
where `y = f(x)` is the DB time for a source time `x`. In the simple
case where `f` is just the identity this gives us the behaviour we had
before.

* In the interim, to reduce impact on user code, we will make use of
a thin layer of glue to make it behave more like before (in terms of
API and structure of the main loop) until we can provide the
optimiser.

## Decision: ### Command Tests
- Unit-test your commands (the command files themselves).
- Write feature tests for your commands that ensure that they are properly
wired up and integrated into the overall CLI codebase. These tests should be
placed in the command suite, e.g. `command/v7/suite_test.go`.
- If the feature being tested is very large, feel free to give it its own
suite, e.g. `command/v7/ssh_suite_test.go`. The test itself should be
placed in the command suite.

### Integration Tests
- Place all other tests in the integration suite. This includes features that
do not explicitly need to be in the command test suite.
- Integration test suite tests should have as few test cases as possible, and
each test case should have as few `It`s as possible. Each test case should
focus on a single thing.
- Prefer testing new features via acceptance tests (e.g. `acceptance/v7/isolated/`)
whenever possible.
- If there is no specific use case for it being in its own test case, add
tests to `acceptance/v7/isolated/plugin_repository/`.
- If you run into issues with the number of `It`s being tested in acceptance,
isolate your tests as necessary, and use this file for guidance.

## Decision: **Alternative 1**
* `+` The server don't needs a the *client ID* and *secret* to get the access token. 
    * *client ID* and *secret* could not be exposed by the server. 
* `-` When accessing the private repositories from the server (e.g. for downloading content, or listing the accessible repositories), the access token needs to be send to the server.
    * This means, the client still has the access token and would be able to misuse it for malicious purposes by calling GitHub in its name.  

**Alternative 2**
* `+` Only the server has access to the access token and can misuse it.
    * Client does not know the access token and therefore cannot misuse it.
* `-` The server needs a *client ID* and *secret* to get the access token.
    * The server might be vulnerable against attacks (e.g. by exposing *client ID* and *secret* in logfiles)
* `-` **Cannot use this alternative!**
    * It is not possible to call GitHub's [Authorization URL](https://developer.github.com/v3/oauth/#web-application-flow) from the server.
    * Only GitHub can redirect the browser to the application by sending the URL as HTTP response.  

**Alternative 3**
* `+` Client does not know the access token and therefore cannot misuse it.
* `+` Server does know the access token and can misuse it, but is more difficult to misuse.
    * *client ID* and *secret* might be exposed through attacks.

## Decision: We will **duplicate the data** in the reading side as **normalized data** and use a suitable data storage to access it.

Data duplication is part of CQRS to provide better performance and better fit for reading requests that writing requests.

## Advantages

- The reading side uses the data storage tailored to its querying requirements, so there is no need to write a complex ORM to project normalized data from the writing side.  
- The reading side is decoupled from the writing side, so we can change the internal implementation of reading and writing parts independently. This is useful for scaling applications, e.g. for creating and hosting several reading models, that are tailored to the different use cases,
- Optimized database performance, e.g. using index for normalized data,
- Can support real time synchronization - the reading model will be updated immediately (right after saving the data to writing part).  
- Good for the cases where the performance of queries is not so important and the reading model is not updated very often.
- Can be useful for generating reports and different dashboards. 

## Disadvantages

- **Higher complexity** - we need to create 2 data storages.  
- Data synchronization is more complicated.  
- Costly due to higher complexity.

> If it's a simple CRUD application, you do not need CQRS!

## Decision: * Aggregates MUST return an error if `AggregateRoot()` is called for

  function `dogma.StatelessAggregate()`).

  This `StatelessRoot` does not attempt to unmarshal event messages to
  construct the aggregate's state.

  Engines MUST NOT attempt to load data for stateless aggregates.

* Registered nil processes return a special type of `process.StatelessRoot()`
  (note that this was previously a general function `dogma.StatelessProcess()`).

  This `StatelessRoot` does not attempt to unmarshal event messages to
  construct the process' state.

  Engines MUST NOT attempt to load data for stateless processes.

## Decision: The Light Node should run inside a Tendermint-compatible process.
To achieve this, we can reuse [the main command line package `cmd`](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/tree/master/cmd)
used to run the full node. This is very well-defined,
and already provides support for:

- config file
- command line flags
- logging
- RPC

We simply need to provide a new command, like `start`, `testnet`, `init`,
which can be `start-light`.

Within the Tendermint process, we should have a package named `node`
which defines the `LightNode` as a `Service`
(see https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/blob/master/libs/service/service.go).
This service package contains a few utility functions that are used by the
mainTendermint package to manage the main application loop,
including `Start`, `Stop`, and error handling.
It also provides an interface for `Service`.
The top-level `LightNode` will then be composed of some of the pieces shown
in the diagram in [Context](#Context), eg:

```go
type LightNode struct {
  service.Service
  Config *cfg.Config // tendermint config (includes light config)

  // top-level components
  RPC *rpcserver.RPCServer // rpc servers
  Mempool *mempool.Mempool
  EvidencePool *evidence.EvidencePool
  BlockchainReactor *blockchain.BlockchainReactor
  ConsensusReactor *consensus.ConsensusReactor
  P2PReactor *p2p.P2PReactor
  LightReactor *light.LightReactor
  LightClient *lc.Client
  StateReactor *state.StateReactor

  // state
  Store          sm.Store       // the store
  State          sm.State       // the latest committed state
  BlockStore     bs.BlockStore  // the block store (only keep headers)
  PeerStates     *P2PPeerStates // information about each peer
  GenDoc         *types.GenesisDoc
  EventBus       *mp.EventBus   // all events go here
  Cdc            *wire.Codec

  // other
  txs       chan abci.ResponseDeliverTx // channel for receiving results of DeliverTx
  votesync  bool // whether or not to sync or vote
  privValidator types.PrivValidator // for signing votes

  // and some more ...
}

func (n *LightNode) OnStart() error {
  // connect and start rpc
  // start p2p, reactors, etc.
}

func (n *LightNode) OnStop() error {
  // connect and start rpc
  // stop p2p, reactors, etc.
}
```

The config object will contain some new parameters required by
the light node, along the lines of this:

```
# Configuration parameters for light client
[light]

# Max number of blocks that light client can sync without verification
# Only used when trusting period is disabled. 0 means disabled
# Max amount of header requests per peer to prevent peers from spamming our node by sending empty responses
unverified-sync-cap = 0
unverified-max-reqs = 3
```

This way, most of the logic in the LightNode can be handled by
existing packages, and there is a clear place for any LightNode specific
packages, like `light-client`, `light-reactor`, etc.

## Decision: We will record our decisions in this repository in the form of Architectural
Decisions Records (ADRs). These will be recorded in Markdown (as `.md` files) in
the `/docs/decisions/` folder.

We will use a format heavily influenced by Michael Nygard and the [Software
Engineering Institute](https://sew.cmu.edu/process/acquisition-docs/saam.cfm):

- Each ADR is given a 4-digit number to order them numerically;
- Each ADR describes a **Decision**, its **Context**, **Alternatives** and the
  **Consequences** of taking the decision.

We will record an ADR for all decisions we think are worth recording. These will
typically be decisions that:

- influence the platform’s **technical direction**;
- define **conventions** we want to adopt for building applications on the
  platform;
- define **processes** that are critical to operating the platform
  effectively.

We are not going to record ADRs for decisions that do not have any implications
outside of their immediate area.

We will keep ADRs as succinct as possible.

We will aim to record an ADR *before* we implement a decision. This will ensure
that we fully understand its context, alternatives and consequences before we
begin any work.

Once a decision has been taken and ADR has been written, we will leave it
unchanged to act as a historical record. If we subsequently change our minds
and make a different decision, we will record a separate ADR and link to the
previous one in the **Context** section.

We will not try to decide in advance exactly what to record in an ADR. Our
approach to this may evolve over time.

## Decision: To achieve this, `AggregateCommandScope` and `ProcessCommandScope` have been
augmented with a new method, `InstanceExists()`, that returns a boolean
indicating whether or not the instance already exists.

`InstanceExists()` should return `false` before `Create()` has been called, or
after `Destroy()` (for an aggregate) or `End()` (for a process) has been called.

It should return `true` between a successful call to `Create()` and a call to
`Destroy()` or `End()`.

It must return the same value within the same scope.

Note that `InstanceExists()` returns a value indicating whether an instance
_exists_, not whether or not the instance can be _operated upon_. An aggregate
that was previously created but subsequently destroyed, for example, _exists_ but
cannot be interacted with.

### Engine Implementations

To ensure that the value of `InstanceExists()` remains constant within a scope,
it should be computed and stored at the beginning of the scope (before any
operations on the instance are performed).

```scala
package uk.gov.hmrc.hmrcfrontend.views.ImplicitConversions

import uk.gov.hmrc.hmrcfrontend.views.html.components._

/**
  * Provides implicit conversions to wrap simple elements in boilerplate code
  */
trait ImplicitConversions {

  implicit def text(content: String): Text = Text(content)
  implicit def fieldset(legend: Legend): Fieldset = Fieldset(legend = Some(legend))
  implicit def legend(content: Text): Legend = Legend(content = content, classes = "govuk-fieldset__legend--l", isPageHeading = true)

}

object ImplicitConversions extends ImplicitConversions
```

For the following reasons, the decision is to use implicit conversions to simplify the construction of some components.

* The conversion is a conversion to an object (i.e. `Text`, `Legend`, etc.) which has meaning elsewhere (e.g., in a template), rather than to an object which has no particular meaning and simply serves the purpose of being converted back into the original object
* The conversion is a conversion between types which is common and obvious and that will not result in developers encountering confusing circumstances where `String` is being converted to `Text` without them understanding that this conversion has occurred
* The converted object has no state which can lead to unexpected consequences, only a `String` content
* We will only create implicit conversions to fill gaps in play-frontend-hmrc where excessive boilerplate is preventing the development of a usable API for common use cases

For example, to convert `GovukRadio(items: Seq[RadioItem])` to `GovukRadio` where the `id`, `name`, `fieldset`, and `classes` are all generated:

```scala
implicit def radiosWithLegend(items: Seq[RadioItem])(
 implicit messagesApi: MessagesApi, lang: Lang, applicationProvider: ApplicationProvider): GovukRadios = {
    GovukRadios(
      id = Some(items.head.id.getOrElse(throw new IllegalStateException("ID not found on first radio button. Please provide an ID for at least the first radio button"))),
      name = items.head.name.orElse(throw new IllegalStateException("ID not found on first radio button. Please provide an name for at least the first radio button")),
      items = items,
      fieldset = Some(Fieldset(legend = Some(Legend(
        content = Text(items.head.messageForLegend.getOrElse(throw new IllegalStateException("Legend message key not found on first radio button. Please provide a message key for at least the first radio button"))),
        isPageHeading = true,
        classes = "govuk-fieldset__legend--l"
      )))),
      classes = "govuk-radios--inline"
    )
  }

implicit def radios(items: Seq[RadioItem])(
 implicit messagesApi: MessagesApi, lang: Lang, applicationProvider: ApplicationProvider): GovukRadios = {
    GovukRadios(
      id = Some(items.head.id.getOrElse(throw new IllegalStateException("ID not found on first radio button. Please provide an ID for at least the first radio button"))),
      name = items.head.name.orElse(throw new IllegalStateException("ID not found on first radio button. Please provide an name for at least the first radio button")),
      items = items
    )
  }
```

The implicit conversion is more complicated here as it involves generating IDs, names and fieldset components that have not been provided by the developer. It is also not always obvious when it would be invoked - there are two ways to invoke it and there is no guarantee that they would always produce the same result depending on what imports have been included in the current scope.

In this instance, a `Seq[RadioItem]` should be converted to `GovukRadios` by using a simple helper function. For example:

```scala

      GovukRadios(
        name = name,
        id = Some(id),
        fieldset = Some(Fieldset(legend = Some(Legend(content = Text(legend), classes = classes, isPageHeading = isPageHeading)))),
        items = radios
      )

## Decision: We will use Architecture Decision Records, as [described by Michael Nygard](http://thinkrelevance.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions) to record our architectural decisions and the tradeoffs made in getting to a particular solution. This makes it easier for new people coming on to a project to gain an understanding and contributes towards keeping the team a productive as possible.

## Decision: -  We will separate our code by functionality into individual, installable, and
   reusable units. The individual functions of a component should be clearly
   separated, such that the concerns of <u>any single component can be completely
   ignored</u> when considering the concerns of <u>any other single
   component</u>.

1.  This design principle should be applied to each and every package in a given
    application (whether that application consists of a single repository,
    multiple repositories, or a combination).

1.  **"Loose coupling" is preferred.** Modules should be designed with the
    intention of limiting or preventing communication between modules.

### Modular Architecture with the Monorepo

We manage multiple packages in a monorepo approach with Lerna to manage
dependencies and build operations across the modules. Lerna also makes a
monorepo more understandable and more manageable to maintain.

With Lerna, we can do these things:

-   Add and remove packages
-   Add and remove dependencies between the packages
-   Update all dependencies with the latest versions (via npm)
-   Execute scripts at the root level and within a package
-   Execute any npm command within any of the packages, or within all of them

### Module Layout within the Monorepo

In the `packages/` directory, every subdirectory represents an individual
package. The packages are organized by their <u>functional</u> rather than their
<u>technical</u> purpose, as this makes the directory and module structure more
readable and understandable.

#### Monorepo Structure

```text
.
├── packages/                                       All packages located here
│   ├── Package A                                   Package A
│   │   ├── package.json                            Package.json of Package A
│   │   └── src                                     Source code of Package A
│   │       └── PackageA.ts                         Main file for Package A
│   └── Package B                                   Package B
│       ├── package.json                            Package.json of Package B
│       └── src
│           ├── types.ts                            Definition file
│           └── index.ts                            Main file for Package B
└── package.json                                    Root package.json
```

#### Module Naming

To ensure unique naming on npm, the packages are prefixed with
`@archetypes-rules` (as a namespaced package), e.g. `@archetypes-rules/packagea`

### Dependency Management

#### Common Tooling

The packages are developed with a common toolset to ensure the maintainability
of the monorepo. This allows us to share common tooling and configurations
between the packages in a very transparent way. This applies for tools such as:

-   TypeScript
-   ESlint
-   Prettier
-   Jest

#### Versioning

All packages use the same version, and are versioned with Lerna.

#### Typescript

Typescript is configured via a `tsconfig.json` at the monorepo root. Each
package includes its own `tsconfig.json`, inheriting from the root config. The
packages include only the files relevant to the specific package.

### Build process

Every package can be built separately; every package has its own `build` script
in its `package.json`. Lerna executes all build scripts of the packages in the
correct order (from no dependencies up to the most dependencies).

Lerna runs the dependencies of a given package first. So if Package B depends
on Package A, then Lerna will build Package A first, followed by Package B.

### Release and Publish

Releasing and publishing packages is achieved with the help of Lerna. Lerna
does the following tasks automatically:

-   Determines which packages have changed
-   Increments the version of the changed packages and their dependents
-   Creates a new release on GitHub
-   Publishes the packages to npm

This can be done with the command `lerna version`. For more information, see the
[Lerna](https://github.com/lerna/lerna) documentation.

### Other References

-   <https://github.com/nxorg/nx>
-   <https://github.com/babel/babel/blob/master/doc/design/monorepo.md>
-   <https://engineering.atspotify.com/2016/11/04/how-we-use-google-s-monorepo-model-for-android-development/>
-   <https://medium.com/@j0rd_r/what-is-a-mono-repo-monorepos-explained-75394ef342>

## Decision: We will generalize our current system of Organization, FacilityGroup, and Facility into a single tree-like hierarchy of `Region`s. Each `Region` in the hierarchy has a name, a description, and an associated type (Organization, State, Block, etc). Each region can have children regions, but no region has multiple parents. This hierarchy will look roughly as follows:

- *Organization*
    - *State*
        - *District* 
            - *Block*
                - *Facility*

A region can refer either to a grouping of facilities or to an individual facility. The `Region` table in the database will have an optional foreign key that links it to a `Facility` table. All records will ultimately refer to the relevant facility, via foreign key and also via region_slug.

For syncing the mobile app, we will use the `Block` region type. A user's device will sync all patients and records for the block in which that user has most recently logged in. If that block does not have any records -- for instance, in the case of a new block without any patient registration -- the app will fall back to syncing the entire district. 

### Current Data Model (simplified)

```mermaid
classDiagram
class Organization {
    - UUID id
    - string name
}
class FacilityGroup {
    - UUID id
    - string name
    - UUID organization_id
}
class Facility {
    - UUID id
    - string name
    - UUID facility_group_id
}
Organization "1" -- "*" FacilityGroup
FacilityGroup "1" -- "*" Facility
```

### Proposed Data Model

```mermaid
classDiagram
class Region {
    - UUID id
    - string name
    - string type
    - text description
    - boolean sync_enabled
    - UUID parent_id
    - UUID facility_id
}
class RegionType {
    - UUID id
    - string name
    - UUID parent_id
}
class Facility {
    - UUID id
    - string name
}
Region "1" -- "*" Region
Region "1" -- "0..1" Facility
```

Each record will still ultimately refer to the facility ID and region ID associated with it. 

### Data Migration

We can transform our existing model into a region hierarchy by following these rules:

- All Organizations become `Region` of type `Organization`.
- All FacilityGroups become `Region` of type `District`.
- All Facilities become `Region` of type `Facility`, and their `region_id` field will link back to their facility UUID.

In order to support Block-level syncing, we will need to add new `Region` of type `Block`. We can do this by using a GIS boundary file. India, where Simple is primarily active, has good GIS data at the Block level which we can use to map the Facilities to their respective Blocks.

Since records will still be stored with a `Facility` field, we'll need to add a `Region` field to each record that corresponds to the `Region` with a type `Facility`. This will link a record to the corresponding facility's location in the new region hierarchy.

## Decision: Adopt the use of an Enterprise Data Warehouse. A typical approach for setting a data warehouse is to choose between a schema that is driven by the data structures in the operational systems that we're using, which is typically described as being normalized, or a schema that's specifically designed to support analytical reporting and is driven by the business questions that the reports need to answer. 

Although a normalized schema may be tempting since it doesn't involve as much work up front, and the data is similar to how it exists in the sources we have, it's not well suited for reporting and ad hoc analysis, as data is spread out, making it hard to query and requiring extensive join conditions. This also implies additional processing which leads to increased report execution times. Furthermore, adding new source systems to a normalized schema also means that some existing reports might need to be rewritten.

A dimensional schema is the solution to these problems. This type of schema relies on using dimensions, which provide the ability to answer business questions, and fact tables, which provide the information that is used to evaluate the answers to those questions. Even though a dimensional model might take some effort to develop at first, the benefits of using one will certainly outweigh the effort involved. It's much easier to implement and use, and provides the ability to expand the data warehouse with more data sources and/or more data with minimum effort involved. 

So with this in mind, and the fact that we have good reasons to adopt the use of a dimensional model based on Ralph Kimball's approach, this is our chosen solution for the data warehouse schema.

test the code. This will help to reduce the complexity and runtime of our testing
pipeline. Integration tests have their place, but should be used sparingly because
of the difficulty in writing, running, and maintaining them.

## Decision: Whenever possible, entities should be rendered using cached markup instead of sending requests to the Termbox (v2) service on every request.

The preferred solution is to implement a `ParserCache` extension that manages dedicated cache keys in the `ParserCache` with their content generated by the external Termbox (v2) service.  
Such an extension would intercept MediaWiki's `ParserOutput` construction and replace the user-specific Termbox (v2) results with markers before adding the page to the `ParserCache`.  
A MediaWiki hook that allows such an extension to replace a marker in the page before rendering is currently [under review for MediaWiki 1.33](https://gerrit.wikimedia.org/r/c/mediawiki/core/+/470876).

Such a `ParserCache` extension would take into account the "entity", "entity revision" and "interface language" dimension in its keys.

This option was chosen because  

* it drastically reduces the load on the Termbox (v2) service
* the amount of user-specific markup to be generated live on the first request for the 98%+ of logged-out users is kept at a minimum
* it keeps the complexity within the `TermboxRenderingIntegration` service in Wikibase itself to a minimum  

This option was chosen in despite of the current lack of a MediaWiki extension hook to implement the logic for replacing the placeholder in the page before it's rendered, based on the assumption that such a hook will be available soon.

### Alternative considered: Rely entirely on HTTP caching

A [study done in November 2018 by Wikimedia](https://phabricator.wikimedia.org/T210167) suggests that 95% of traffic to mediawiki.org are served by HTTP proxies. In these scenarios, the request would not even reach MediaWiki's `ParserCache`.

To leverage this, Wikibase could implement a HttpCache extension that replaces the Wikibase markup for the Termbox (v2) section of the page with a Placeholder before sending the page to the browser.
On the browser, some Javascript would then fetch the markup using AJAX from a dedicated endpoint in Wikibase and insert it into the page. The response to the AJAX request would again be cacheable by HTTP proxies.

This option was rejected because:

* we don't have good metrics to support the notion that this option would be better
* it has additional complexity:
  * Javascript to do the fetching and inserting
  * additional endpoint to server the request
* search engines generally don't execute JS before rendering the page, meaning the page content will be invisible to them

## Decision: All data should be stored on the DA layer.

At the lowest layer is the Rollkit Block, which is just a single DA block of arbitrary height and data. Each DA block contains 1 Rollkit block. The Rollkit Block will be wrapped in the DA layer's native representation.

The header of the Rollkit block holds all the data to maintain a chain. Each DA block will contain 1 header. The DA layer will determine how many transactions can be placed inside each block given their transaction size.

### DA block

- DA Height: Height of DA layer containing the block (uint)
- DA Hash: The hash of the DA block  (bytes)

### Rollkit Block

- DA Height: (uint)
- DA Hash: (bytes)
- Header
  - Version: (uint)
  - NamespaceID: unique identifier for the namespace of the blockchain (namespace.ID)
  - DA Height: the height of the DA block. Used in order to support DA layers that allow re-indexing of headers or DA layers that might return headers with differing orderings.
  - Time: timestamp of the Block, in seconds since UNIX Epoch, stored as an int64 (signed)
  - Last Block ID (BlockID)
    - Hash: The hash of the previous Rollkit block header (Hash)
    - Height: Height of the previous Rollkit block. Note that this height may not be equal to DA Height + 1 when blocks are empty (uint)
    - Signature: If block data is stored in a separate blob of the same DA block this signature is used as authentication (byte[])
  - Block Data Root: The root hash of all block data that is stored in the same DA block. If empty, the Merkle roots of the block data should be 0s, and the DA layer will return an empty block. (Hash)
  - Transaction Merkle Root: Root hash of Merkle tree of Rollkit transactions (Hash)
  - Data Commitment: (Hash)
  - Last Commit Merkle Root: Root hash of Merkle tree of Tendermint CommitInfo from Rollkit Block at Header.LastBlockID.Height.
  - State Merkle Root: Root hash of Merkle tree of the application state (Hash)

### BlockID

- Hash: The hash of the header of the Rollkit Block
- Height: The height of the header of the Rollkit Block
- Signature: (byte[])

### Hash

- sha256 of the Block header, or root hash of a Merkle tree (byte[32])

### Merkle Trees

Merkle trees are structured like so:
- First level: leaves
- Second level: hash of pairs of adjacent leaves. If a row has odd number of elements, the last leaf will be paired with itself.
- Continue hashing adjacent pairs until a root hash is generated.
- All hashes are SHA256, so all roots are of byte[32]

We will use the existing [Tendermint Merkle tree](https://docs.tendermint.com/v0.34/spec/core/data_structures.html#block-header). Merkle leaves are hashed (SHA256) before they are hashed with their neighbors.

Rollkit header merkle tree structure:
- Block Data Root: (Hash)
- Transaction Merkle Root: (Hash)
- Data Commitment: (Hash)
- Last Commit Merkle Root: (Hash)
- State Merkle Root: (Hash)

### Transaction

Transactions consist of a byte array (byte[]) of data and a signature (byte[])

### Last Commit

The Tendermint CommitInfo structure will be used.

### State

Application State, which can be defined arbitrarily (byte[])

## Decision: ### Background
According to [Google Cloud Function's
documentation](https://cloud.google.com/functions/docs/writing/accepted-signatures),
there is not one uniform signature for a cloud function's entry point.
Developers are free to use either 1, 2, or 3 arguments. A cloud function can
be asynchronous (triggered by a Cloud PubSub topic) or synchronous (triggered by an
HTTP request). The number of arguments is depending on whether the function is an
HTTP function and/or has an associated context. Below, we give the details in a
table.

| Trigger type/Arguments | 0 arguments | 1 argument (HTTPRequest object) | 1 argument (CloudEvent object) | 2 arguments (Data and context) | 3 arguments (Data, context and callback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HTTP trigger | Possible | Possible (recommended) | Not possible | Not possible | Not possible |
| PubSub trigger | Possible | Not possible | Possible (recommended) | Possible | Possible (not possible without a callback) |

From the table we can conclude the best way to handle PubSub functions is
asynchronous, because it is the way to add a callback to the function.
Therefore, this will be our recommended approach for PubSub functions.

### How to use a Cloud function 

#### **Python**

- Synchronous PubSub functions

``` python
    def hello_world(event, context):
        """triggered by a Pubsub topic.
        Args:
            event (dict): Event payload.
            context (google.cloud.functions.Context): Metadata for the event.
        """
        # Do a bunch of useful things here
```

- Asynchronous PubSub functions

  - With return value

    ``` python
    def hello_world_asynchronous_with_callback(event, context, callback):
        """triggered by a Pubsub topic.
        Args:
            event (dict): Event payload.
            context (google.cloud.functions.Context): Metadata for the event.
            callback (function): Function to call after all is done.
        """
        # Do a bunch of useful things here
        # Return the following
        callback()
    ```

    With an optional success value for the callback function

    ``` python
    def hello_world_asynchronous_with_success_callback(event, context, callback):
        """triggered by a Pubsub topic.
        Args:
            event (dict): Event payload.
            context (google.cloud.functions.Context): Metadata for the event.
            callback (function): Function to call after all is done.
        """
        # Do a bunch of useful things here
        # Return the following
        # True is used as a succes value for the callback function
        callback(True)
    ```

  - With `async`

    ``` python
    async def hello_world_asynchronous_async(event, context):
        """triggered by a Pubsub topic.
        Args:
            event (dict): Event payload.
            context (google.cloud.functions.Context): Metadata for the event.
        """
        # Do a bunch of useful things here
    ```

    Note that an asynchronous function uses a specific [client library](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/functions-framework-python).

#### **JavaScript**

- Synchronous PubSub functions

  - With return value

    ``` javascript
    /**
     * Responds to any HTTP request.
     * @param {!Object} req HTTP request object.
     * @param {!Object} res HTTP response object.
     */
    exports.helloWorld_sync_return = (event, context) => {
        // Do a bunch of useful things here
        // Return the following
        return 'success'
    };
    ```

  - With `Promise`

    ``` javascript
    /**
     * Responds to any HTTP request.
     * @param {!Object} req HTTP request object.

## Decision: Relying parties must perform the following validity checks:

1. Validate the certificate used to sign the assertion. It must be
   valid and trusted
1. Validate the signature of the assertion using the public key of the
   certificate
1. Validate that the assertion is not expired: `NotOnOrAfter` from the
   subject confirmation data, and `NotOnOrAfter` and `NotBefore` from
   the conditions block (the MSA never sends the latter)
1. Assert that the recipient of the subject confirmation data is correct
   (it must point to your ACS)
1. Assert that the `InResponseTo` of the subject confirmation data is
   correct (it must refer to your `request_id` for that particular
   transaction)
1. Assert that your own entity ID (the SP's) is in the list of
   audiences for which the assertion was issued
1. Assert that the issuer of the assertion (the MSA) is the one you
   expect
1. Assert that the AuthnContextClassRef indicates that a Level 2
   authentication took place (unless your service explicitly states that
   Level 1 is sufficient)
1. Assert that the assertion is a SAML v2.0 assertion
1. Assert that the subject's NameID has a persistent format, as shown in the example above

## Decision: ### Use `core::error::Error` for errors in `core` crates that were created only to encapsulate errors of other crates

### Use `Error` from `core::error` for errors that can happen in the code

All of the functions that can return `Error` have to have type `Result<T, Error>`. No other error types should be returned from them.
Also, there shouldn't be any custom error types in the code, except for `Error` type used in every `ockam_*` crate.
It can be instantiated in the simplest way by calling constructor without arguments:
```
return Err(Error::default())
```

It can be customized a bit by calling `new` or `new_with_message` constructors:
```
return Err(Error::new(kind))
```

```
return Err(Error::new_with_message(kind, message))
```

And it can also use `From` implementation for standard library errors, with `Core` error kind:
```
return res.map_err(|e| Error::from(e))
```

### Map error codes on a separate layer

Each type of module will have an error code range specified in `core::error::errors` to map the module-specific errors to their corresponding error kinds.

The following error code ranges are proposed:

- 0-255: Core (used in `core` crate)
- 256-511: Local storage
- 512-767: Transport (network and IoT devices)
- 768-1023: Remote storage
- 1024-1279: Management
- 1280-1535: Encryption
- 1536-1791: Remote management
- 1792-2047: Protocol
- 2048-2303: Third-party or library errors

## Decision: ### REST Endpoints

1. Endpoints should generally conform to what has become the industry de facto standard convention of creating them by composing the resource noun with the applicable action. So, an operation to delete a person would generally be a `DELETE` request to `/person/{personId}`. The resource noun would be plural when dealing with collections and singular when working with individual resources.
2. In general, all REST endpoints should return JSON.
3. Errors should always return an HTTP 500 status code unless they are the result of invalid or missing request parameters. In the case of missing or invalid request parameters, a 400 (Bad Request) or 422 (Unprocessable Entity) status code may be appropriate.
4. Error responses must include an array of error objects that include a numeric error code and a string error message describing the problem.
5. Error responses may include an optional `developerMessage` that contains additional context relevant to the problem from a developer's perspective. It may contain additional exception or stack trace details, but this information should not be returned in production environments.
6. Error responses may include an optional array of `links` that may contain additional information describing the error.
7. Where there is no response, we should return the 204 (No Content) status code.

## Decision: We are going to use option 3 and use the AWS SDK to provide signed URLs.

Each URL provides access to the specified S3 Object for a fixed time.

This will put the burden of retries and bandwidth on the client, and off the server. It also reduces API latency, as we don't have to wait for the whole file to upload to the server, and the connection can terminate when we return the signed URL.

Additionally, our current API implementation uses [Django Ninja][Django Ninja]. This doesn't directly support multipart file uploads, though we could use [DRF's `MultiPartParser`][DRF MultiPartParser] which appears compatible. However, it seems safer to rely on the AWS SDK and keep the API implementation as clean as possible.

[Django Ninja]: https://django-ninja.rest-framework.com/
[DRF MultiPartParser]: https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/parsers/#multipartparser

## Decision: ### Commit history
* A commit history must be a history of features and fixes.
* Merge commits are prohibited.
* Each commit should represent a unit of work. For feature development, a unit of work represents a step to implement that feature. The last commit should leave a working feature behind.
* During the work, a developer can commit to the branch arbitrarily often, e.g. after a task is completed, as part of a task, etc. Those commits should be merged after the review into the branch using rebase and squash or interactive rebase.
* The squashed commit history should tell the whole story of the feature or bugfix. This simplifies the review and helps in future debugging.

### Commit message format
* Use `[Type]: Short description (100 characters max)` format.
  * Types:
    * `feat` for a new feature
    * `fix` for a bug fix
    * `docs` for documentation only changes
    * `refactor` for a code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature
    * `test` for adding missing tests or correcting existing tests
    * `chore` for repository maintenance
    * `style` for changes that do not affect the meaning of the code (white-space, formatting, missing semi-colons, etc.)
  * Description should be written in [imperative mood](https://www.atlassian.com/blog/git/what-a-great-git-commit-message-looks-like): _"Fix bug"_, not _"Fixed bug"_ or _"Fixes bug"_
* A commit message should have a blank second line.
* For complex commits add a blank third line and an extended description explaining your changes.
  The description should be wrapped to 100 characters.

## Decision: We introduce a `Headers` class representing a map of string to string headers and provide 2 merging strategies for it.
Merge strategy A will be used for combining headers set by the user (SDK related or custom) and will follow these rules:

1. Keys will be case-insensitive
2. Case of the key will be preserved and will be that of the first encountered key (first is highest priority)
3. For values, the value of the first encountered header will be used
4. Merged value will be encoded.

Merge strategy B will be used for combining headers created by the destination and connectivity services.
This can also combine header names with the same name, as can happen when combining additional headers and proxy headers from the destination.
These headers will not be encoded but can contain values encoded with [RFC2047](https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2047) by the destination service.
The strategy for merging these values:
1. Merge values of same name in `Authorization` header
2. Merge same name headers of all others by concatenation with `,` separator.

**OData**
Merge strategy A for custom and SDK related (eTag and cookies) headers to be performed upon request building, merging headers in this order: cookie header (cookies are from previous responses so it makes sense for it to have lowest prio), custom headers, etag header.
Merge strategy B to be performed when combining headers from destinations, proxy and tenant specific auth.

Query Parameters will be handled in a similar way for version 2, but will follow this merge order: destination related query parameters, custom query parameters, SDK related query parameters.

**OpenAPI**
Custom headers will be handled in a similar fashion for version 1 and 2: Merge custom and SDK related custom (SDK related custom only for Version 2: cookies) headers using merge strategy A.
Merge strategy B to be performed when combining headers from destinations, proxy and tenant specific auth.

SDK related query parameters in this ADR refers to parameters that are set by the request config / request builder.

**Version 1**:
- Open API: mergeStrategy A is implemented in a different fashion. It is done with lodash's merge, which leads to issues for arrays and values not being RFC2047-encoded by the request (in destination service). All other headers, which is essentially only the SDK related are merged after custom. We will change the merge to use our new `Headers` class.
- OData: mergeStrategy A is implemented for SDK related and custom headers. For SDK headers and etag custom headers merge: all custom headers are merged and then combined with the etag header so custom headers take precedence over the eTag. cookies are currently not handled. Merge strategy B does not distinguish between Authorization and other headers.

**Version 2**:
- Open API: mergeStrategy A will follow the following merge order: cookie header, custom headers, custom SDK headers.
- OData: mergeStrategy A will follow the following merge order: cookie header, custom headers, eTag header.
- For all SDK related query parameters in OData we will use the `Headers` class with the appropriate merging order: destination related query parameters, custom query parameters and SDK related query parameters.

| SDK Version | OpenAPI | OData |
|-------------|---------|-------|
| 1.0         | Custom, proxy, destination, tenant-specific, client. Proxy, destination and tenant specific are all part of the destination. All of these headers are treated equally and merged with the same strategy | Custom, etag, cookies, proxy, destination, tenant-specific, client. All the destination related headers are treated equally and merged with the same strategy |
| 2.0         | Custom, cookies, proxy, destination, tenant-specific | Custom, cookies, etag, proxy, destination, tenant-specific |
| ADR         | Custom, cookies, custom-SDK, destination. custom-SDK means here additional headers and proxy from the destination | Custom, cookies, etag, destination |

Custom-SDK only means here "AdditionalHeaders" and "ProxyHeader".

To implement and deliver the "Composites" component in a piecemeal fashion:

  be supported, followed by Office documents, Video, ZIP, Email & PDF
  attachments.
* Each phase of a given pipeline can be disabled. For example, a
  document repository could provide a document that contains image
  content but does not want to support full-text search.  In such a
  case, the OCR and Full-Text extraction phases can be disabled.
* Each phase of a given pipeline could be optionally executed against a
  worker process from another DLCS (see below).

This approach will be adopted as each object type requires a distinct
processing pipeline. Office documents and PDF share a number of
similarities in their initial extraction, but the later phases such as
full-text extraction are very different. Videos require a
video-to-image extraction component, email requires a mail parser
component and attachments have to be handled on an individual
basis. Supporting all of this in a single worker process is likely to
prove unmanageable as the overall codebase will not be divided into
sensible logical units, but according to the phase that is currently
being executed. Also, it is conceivable that specific phases such as
text extraction and image extraction could become highly configurable,
and we do not want to mix the two concepts together such that a change
for PDF also affects Office documents.

The alternative approach of each processing component having its own
dedicated pipeline (i.e. we don't have separate pipelines for the
different object types, but individual pipelines for text extraction,
image extraction etc.) was not adopted. The reason for this is that it
would imply having the same component running in multiple contexts and
potentially with a different configuration for each. E.g. we might want
to perform different image extraction when operating against a PDF as
opposed to a Video asset. Although this is not a concern for now, it
seems a sensible approach to keep components and pipelines segregated
so that such distinctions could be made later on.
