## Decision: OpenJDK 8 was the last release from Oracle under the Oracle Binary Code Licence;
Oracle has subsequently adopted the GNU General Public Licence, version 2 + Classpath Exception (GPLv2-CPE) for the Oracle distribution of OpenJDK.
However, Oracle is not alone, and has made commitments to the OpenJDK project to be sure that the community has a vibrant, viable path forward.

### Oracle's Position

With the adoption of the OpenJDK distributions of Java by many organisations, Oracle is now charging for the Oracle JDK with support in a way that is similar to what
it has always done for other Oracle products, such as its Database.

### Industry Position

Industry has responded by either ignoring this, or migrating to other distributions of OpenJDK, the OpenJDK ecosystem. Many are migrating to OpenJDK 11,
or later releases, rather than remain on release 8; as that provides another 10 years of feature and support updates. Some distributions provide support,
and Oracle, and others, provide distributions under the open source licensing.

### Oracle's Distribution of OpenJDK

Oracle also makes an OpenJDK distribution available under GPLv2-CPE (without commercial support). This is the version that can be found at <https://jdk.java.net>.
This distribution includes support for:

* **Java 8** as release 8u262; support for JDK 8 ends in January 2021
* **Java 11** as release 11.0.8; support for JDK 11 ends in January 2022
* **Java 14** as release 14.0.2; support for JDK 14 ends in September 2020

### Community Distribution of OpenJDK 

* **AdoptOpenJDK**: <https://adoptopenjdk.net>
  * Provide supported releases 8 (extended) and 11 (LTS), for various platforms, using HotSpot or OpenJ9 Virtual Machines
  * Offer HotSpot, OpenJ9 and Shenandoah Garbage Collectors; including back-port of Shenandoah to Java 8
  * Provide extended support from various sources, including Oracle

* **Amazon Corretto**: <https://aws.amazon.com/corretto>
  * A no-cost, multiplatform, production-ready distribution of the Open Java Development Kit (OpenJDK)
  * Supports Linux, Windows and macOS
  * Releases 8 (extended) and 11 (LTS)
  * Back-port of various features

* **Azul Zulu**: <https://www.azul.com/downloads/zulu-community>
  * Enterprise-grade, production-ready binary distributions of OpenJDK; certified compliant
  * Supports Linux, Windows, macOS, Android; ARM architectures
  * Releases 6, 7, 8 (extended), 9, 10, 11 (LTS), 12, 13 and 14
  * Include a back-port of Shenandoah to Java 8
  * Provide Enterprise Support

### Community Distribution of Java

* **GraalVM Community Edition**: <https://www.graalvm.org/downloads>
  * A no-cost, multiplatform, production-ready polyglot distribution of the Open Java Development Kit (OpenJDK)
  * Supports Linux, Windows and macOS
  * Releases 8 and 11 (LTS)
  * Includes the GraalVM Compiler, Substrate VM, GraalVM tools; including Ahead-Of-Time and Just-In-Time compilation

GraalVM has a particular use case: when deploying containers, having a pre-compiled (Ahead-Of-Time compiled) native image (application) in the container can reduce both application startup and memory requirements (the two main factors that drive cloud costing in an event-driven architecture).

A feature of GraalVM's SubstrateVM, an Ahead-Of-Time runtime, is the ability to produce these native images from Java Byte Code. These can then be delivered via Docker images that
are much smaller, have reduced startup time and much reduced memory footprint; compared to containers containing a JDK and a Java Byte Code image.

### IITD Architecture Recommendation

IITD Architecture strongly recommend that OpenJDK is deployed throughout the Government of British Columbia, so as to avoid any licensing and support issues.

IITD Architecture further recommend that OpenJDK 11, or later releases, are deployed. As JDK 8 support will cease in January 2021, and JDK 11 is the latest Long Term Support release.
The OpenJDK ecosystem will provide enhanced, longer term support for JDK 11 and later LTS releases.

## Decision: * Resources are referred to by **nouns** in the URI, not verbs.

* Collection names (e.g., `customers`) are preferred over element names (e.g., `customer`). When referring to a single element, its ID is appended to the collection name (e.g., `customers/123`).

* REST resources and actions map to HTTP methods:

| Method   | Read-Only | Safe | Cacheable | Idempotent |
| -------- | :-------: | :--: | :-------: | :--------: |
| GET      |     ✔     |  ✔   |     ✔     |     ✔      |
| POST     |           |      |           |            |
| PUT      |           |      |           |     ✔      |
| PATCH    |           |      |           |     ✔      |
| DELETE   |           |      |           |     ✔      |

The following standard set of HTTP methods should be used for simple REST interactions. Additional methods can be used but might not be correctly handled by certain HTTP clients (e.g., XMLHttpRequest):

* **GET**: Retrieve or list resources.

    A GET request should not be used to create, modify or delete resources.

* **POST**: Create resources, or trigger non-idempotent actions.

    The POST method is often used to trigger actions that are not naturally mapped to another method. Since these actions might perform multiple operations and create non-idempotent results, care must be taken when defining them.

    For example, triggering the approval of an order and having this reflected through an `orderState` property:

    ```text
    POST /orders/123/approve  (this approach)

    PUT /orders/123          (vs. updating the `orderState` property directly)
    {"orderState": "approved"}
    ```

    Both approaches can be used. The second approach (using PUT) can be beneficial as all order state changes are handled by the PUT method, making it easy to create a history for all states (e.g., by logging the PUT requests). However, the POST method might provide a cleaner and clearer way to create a more sophisticated action that also performs other operations, such as notifying other components or services.

* **PUT**: Update or replace resources, or trigger idempotent actions.

    When updating a resource, it must be ensured that it still represents the correct state before applying changes. However, there are different approaches to applying the changes to a resource, which are explained in the [Optimistic Concurrency Control](https://github.com/zalando/rest-api-guidelines/blob/master/zalando-restful-api-guide.md#optimistic-concurrency-control) section.

* **PATCH**: Update parts of a resource.

    The PATCH method should be used for operations such as "update property", "add element to a list", "change properties on a nested object" etc. PATCH requests are typically sent with a `application/json-merge-patch` media type (RFC7396) or `application/json-patch+json` media type (RFC6902), depending on the complexity of the operation. While `application/json-merge-patch` is the easiest to use, RFC7396 states that **server implementations cannot fail-back to replacing with PUT**. So for example, sending an empty payload for a merge patch should *not* cause the server to treat the request as a full replacement, i.e., delete everything and insert nothing. So when replacing resource data where `null` implies delete, the PUT method is still the best.

    Both media types are supported and can be used on a per-API basis; the decision on which one to use is up to the API designer. However, a server must support the merge patch media type when supporting PATCH.

* **DELETE**: Delete resources.

## Decision: A generic “Searches” bounded context will be implemented with ElasticSearch as a backing index for the advanced search functionality required by the use cases. Each bounded context will be able to populate its own index into the Searches bounded context. The Searches bounded context will expose an endpoint to retrieve the required entities that need the advanced search functionality.

More specifically the searches bounded context will expose a generic endpoint in this format:

```
PUT /searches/{SearchIndexName}
```

This endpoint will allow the bounded context that requires the advanced search functionality to set up the mapping and settings that will configure the search index. Each Search Index can contain multiple documents, one for each entity type that requires the advance search functionality.

Then there’s a second generic endpoint in this format:

```
PUT /searches/{SearchIndexName}/documents
```

This endpoint allows the bounded context to load the data that needs to be available in the search index in a simple way (no logic is needed in the Searches bounded context).

Finally the search endpoint is in this format:

```
GET /searches/{SearchIndexName}/{DocumentTypeName}?parameters
```

This endpoint allows the client apps to retrieve the list of entities (DocumentTypeName) from the search index (SearchIndexName) with the search functionality provided by ElasticSearch (e.g. wildcards, partial matching, boolean operators etc). The advanced search features are provided using the elasticsearch “query string query” and the parameters are passed using the URL. The data returned by this endpoint will be the minimal to identify the entity (e.g. entity id, search fields values etc) so that later the client app can use these values to query the domain bounded context to retrieve the full information for the entity.

For the first implementation the Searches bounded context will have to include an endpoint for the advanced search of person/assets tenures; to support the advance search for the person tenure the data needed is coming from 2 bounded contexts, e.g. the person bounded context to retrieve the person name and the assets-tenures bounded context to retrieve the tenure type (fixed terms, periodic etc). So in order to implement the advanced search for the person tenure it will be necessary to update the `GET /searches/PersonTenures` endpoint to perform a join between the person bounded context and the tenure bounded context in a way that’s flexible and easily adaptable for the next search functionality required. Elastic Search offers the Nested Query which allows doing join queries, so a first implementation will be done using this, and it will be updated later if required.

![Searches Bounded Context](./searches-bounded-context.png)

### Positive consequences

- Advance search functionality provided
- Searches functionality is separated into its own bounded context that can be used by other bounded contexts

### Negative consequences

- ElasticSearch adds an extra technology to the Hackney technology stack
- As the Searches bounded context will perform the join queries it will be highly dependent on the domains that provide the information
- It requires the use of ElasticSearch nested query feature

## Decision: * The startup of an Interlok instance should not be stalled by any individual component.
* The application should continue to work and accept configuration changes (from the UI or API) if possible
* The Interlok instance should not be responsible for the scheduling of any state changes
* Component state changes are handled asynchronously by a thread pool and the requesting thread should continue processing without synchronizing on state changes.
* Synchronization and concurrency are the responsibility of the component being changed, and is not the responsibility of the calling code.

This will allow Interlok instances to start up, and accept configuration changes regardless of any connection failures within it's runtime state.
It will mean any component can transition through it's state phases at any time regardless of the state of other components.

## Decision: - Drop the concept of private/global
- All barcodes, whether created by an organization or imported as part of a default set (e.g., from the [Open Barcode API](https://www.openbarcodes.com/)) are available to all organizations
- Barcode values are not unique in this global pool; in this way, barcode values act as a reference for Base Item lookup
- When a Barcode value is found during Inventory Item entry:
  - If a barcode's associated Base Item is in "Available Base Items" then use that Base Item
  - If multiple barcodes' associated Base Item are in "Available Base Items" then use one of those (it's unclear how the exact choice should be made; for now, we'll probably just use the first match)
  - If no barcode's associated Base Items are in "Available Base Items" then
    - Create a new Base Item using the data in the Barcode if there are no existing
      Base Items with that barcode
    - Else use the Base Item with that barcode (again, for now, we'll probably just use the first match)

This solution supports a future design in which Base Items have default values which can be overridden by a barcode if needed, e.g. for an organization to create their own default values for a certain barcode (e.g., for locally sourced produce), or for a specific Item and Barcode set to have some fixed values for (e.g.) UPC code lookup.

This solution does not support a future design in which organizations may want to specify different default values for Base Items associated with a specific Barcode.

It's unclear at present whether Barcodes and Base Items are 1:1, 1:N, or N:M -- this solution leaves that an open question but will force it during implementation (currently they are 1:1, I think.)

A possible future enhancement: when more than one Barcode exists for a given value, or more than one Base Item can be chosen for the barcode value from an organization's list of "Available Base Items," the user is offered a choice of Base Items to use. (This is difficult with the current Barcode entry component.)

## Decision: We should detect if the signature we recover is from a smart contract wallet.

To achieve this, we can make an on-chain call on Polygon to the `getCodeAt` function at the address recovered from the signature (https://docs.alchemy.com/reference/eth-getcode). This function will return `0x` if the address has no code (i.e. is an EOA).

If we find code at the address (i.e. the signature comes from a smart contract wallet), we can query the contract wallet via a smart contract that knows how to parse common contract wallet interfaces and extract the wallet address from the given signer address, as well as the signature.

A common interface across contract wallets is EIP-1271 (https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1271). With EIP-1271, a contract wallet's `isValidSignature` function will return a specific magic value if the signature is valid.

For any signature provided, the first 65 bytes are the signature itself, and the last 32 bytes should be a magic value returned by the contract to indicate that the signature is valid. This magic value should be set to `0x1626ba7e` which corresponds to the ASCII-encoded string `\x16\x26\xBA\x7E` and represents the function `isValidSignature(bytes32 _hash, bytes _signature)` in Solidity.

Once we confirm that a given signature is valid (either because no code exists at the signer's address, or `isValidSignature` on the contract wallet confirms the signature is valid), we then have to pass the correct wallet address to the meta-transaction so it may be processed on-chain successfully.

In order to simplify the solution we will only support the cases where the signature was generated via EIP-1271, and not the cases that require a more complex, wallet specific signature validation. 

### References
- Open Zepplin EIP-1271 implementation https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/5.x/api/utils#SignatureChecker
- Signature verification libraries:
  - https://github.com/0xsequence/sequence.js
  - https://github.com/pimlico-labs/erc-1271

## Decision: For complex data migrations, or any migration that takes a while to run, we should write it as a Rake task and not include it in an ActiveRecord migration.

Complex migrations could include things that require several different queries to calculate the new data value, joining many tables, etc.

Reasons we are choosing to use Rake tasks in these cases:

* If something goes wrong in an ActiveRecord migration, the transaction is rolled back and the database connection drops. This means that data is in a consistent state but there is no record of where the migration failed and it must be run again from the start after the issue has been fixed.
* When working with a large database, migrations can take a long time to run. In a continuous deployment environment, this will block the deployment pipeline and can put strain on the production database, increasing the risk of downtime.
* ActiveRecord migrations may block writes to the production database while they are running (depending on the type of migration). This is another risk factor for production downtime. A Rake task can be written to be tolerant of writes to the production database.
* ActiveRecord migrations cannot be run again if they were only partially successful, for example, if the database became unresponsive mid-way through. A Rake task can be written to be idempotent and retryable.

For any Rake tasks that migrate data, we should also write them in a way that allows us to run them repeatedly, without causing duplicate data. One way to do this is to check a "flag" on each record before running the migration, so that it will only be run once. An alternative approach is to write the task so that it only selects records that have not already been migrated.

When writing data migration Rake tasks, it's also helpful to include:

* A way to see the progress of the migration (e.g. by printing to the console how many records have been migrated at intervals)
* A way to estimate the time required for the task to complete (e.g. by counting how many records will need migrating before running the task, and dividing by how many records are migrated in the first minute of the task run)
* A way to disable a feature flag before running the migration, and enable it after the migration has completed, if necessary

## Decision: * The ALB health check should test to ensure that the Nginx default Vhost, the Vhosts for each active deployment for
 each configured app are present and the underlying apps are responding with 200 responses to the appropriate request path.
* The ALB health check should be configured to use a short interval in order to rapidly fail out of the ALB target group and avoid causing
 elevated 5xx rates. This requires that the checks pass quickly.
* We must avoid using the public ALB URL to send health check requests. The health checks should always be internal.
* An instance's inclusion in an ASG instance protection group should be delayed until the ALB health check passes, and should be revoked if an ALB health check fails.

When the ALB determines the health of the instance with this check, this provides a more accurate view of the instance's ability to serve requests to all 
applications, allowing us to:

* Fail instances out of the ALB target group more rapidly, reducing the instance's 5xx contribution
* Add new instances to an ASG pool with more certainty that those instances are properly configured and working

The ALB health check will not necessarily tell us that the instance is ready to receive requests for a newly-started app for the first time.
This will only be apparent to the ALB if we change the health check request path to include the route for that app. Since we can't be sure
which app/route the ALB check will test, a better solution may be to rely on Nginx 5xx responses for apps that are not yet listening on their ports.

## Decision: * Use Google Protobuf naming guideline from [Google Cloud API design Guide](https://cloud.google.com/apis/design/naming_convention).
    * Service name MUST end with Service, for instance, `UserService`.
    * RPC method MUST use `Verb + Noun` format, for instance, `SayHello` as a method which greets a user.
    * Resource message MUST use `Noun` format, for instance, `User` which represents a user resource.
    * Request message MUST use `Verb + Noun + Request` format, for instance, `SayHelloRequest` as a request message to `SayHello` method.
    * Response message MUST use `Verb + Noun + Response` format, for instance, `SayHelloResponse` as a response message to `SayHello` method.
* Define `Resource + OperationName + Request` for the resource action, and
`Resource + OperationName + Response` for its response. (e.g. `User+Create+Request` to create a new user and `User+Delete+Request` to delete an existing user, etc.)

* Message definition in `repeated` field MUST end with `List` and `Page`, (e.g., `GetUserListResponse` and `Page+Response` should not be defined separately).

## Decision: All paths to the large data storage area will be defined by the `PACE_DATA_LOCATION` [environment variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environment_variable).

Users will need to configure this variable on their system with the correct path before running any scripts that access the network storage.

Developers will test that the environment variable has been set correctly at the start of any script accessing the network storage.

### Testing of the environment variable

Any code that defines a path based on this environment variable will first check that the environment variable is present and will raise an error if not. 

In [Python](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.environ) this will look like:

```python
import os

if 'PACE_DATA_LOCATION' in os.environ:
    data_location = os.environ['PACE_DATA_LOCATION']
else:
    raise NameError('Environment variable PACE_DATA_LOCATION not set')
```

### Installation of the environment variable

On linux / unix environments (including macOS) the variable can be installed by adding the export line to the end of your `~/.bash_profile` or `.bashrc` file. For example:

```bash
export PACE_DATA_LOCATION=/media/PACE-Data
```

(The path in the above example is for demonstration purposes only - please ask for the correct path).

This file is run when the terminal starts up so will need to be reloaded if the change is made with the terminal already open. For example:

```bash
source ~/.bash_profile
```

On Windows environments the variable can be installed from the Control Panel. See [this](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/procthread/environment-variables) page for more info.

### Docker images

Docker images will be configured to load the path from the environment by [mounting](https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/commandline/run/#mount-volume--v) the directory into the container. This should be set up when the docker image is run not when it is built. This is done by adding the -v flag:

```dockerfile
docker run -v ~/PACE-Data/:/media/PACE-Data -ti my_image
```

## Decision: We propose simplifying the capi block element parsing in frontend and dotcom rendering, by reducing the
depth of the nested structure and using a strongly typed model.

We also propose storing the entire block id as the first parameter of the frontend model object, and
using the `blockId` field as the second parameter for dotcom rendering instead of the block number.

The first step in achieving the proposed simplification is to remove the `BodyBlock.content` field and 
replace it with a `BodyBlock.elements` field with the type `List[Element]`.

The current code:

```
new BodyBlock {
  id = b.id,
  blockId = b.blockId,
  content = content,
  bodyHtml = b.bodyHtml
}
```

will be updated to use the proposed `elements` field and be typed.

```
case class BodyBlock(id: String, blockId: String, elements: List[Element])

object BodyBlock {
  def fromBlock(b: Block, elements: List[Element]): BodyBlock = {
    BodyBlock(
      id = b.id,
      blockId = b.blockId,
      elements = elements
    )
  }
}
```

The next step is to use the `elements` field in place of `content` in dotcom rendering.
The current code:

```
val modelBodyBlocks: Seq[dotcom_rendering.ArticleBodyBlock] =
  item.blocks.bodies.map { block =>
    dotcom_rendering.ArticleBodyBlock(
      blockId = block.blockId,
      bodyHtml = block.bodyHtml.trim,
      content = block.content
    )
  }
```

will be simplified to:

```
val modelBodyBlocks: Seq[dotcom_rendering.ArticleBodyBlock] =
  item.blocks.bodies.zipWithIndex.map { case (block, blockNumber) =>
    dotcom_rendering.ArticleBodyBlock(
      blockId = block.blockId,
      bodyHtml = block.bodyHtml.trim,
      content = block.elements
    )
  }
```

We can then update dotcom rendering to match the frontend model:

```
final case class ArticleBodyBlock(
  blockId: String,
  bodyHtml: String,
  elements: List[Element]
)

object ArticleBodyBlock {
  def fromBlock(b: Block, elements: List[Element]): ArticleBodyBlock = {
    ArticleBodyBlock(
      id = b.id,
      blockId = b.blockId,
      elements = elements
    )
  }
}
```

In dotcom rendering we will have to make a decision of which field to use for `key` and `id` in React,
we will use block id for key and block number for id (as this is how it's currently rendered).

We would like to remove the `id` and `bodyHtml` fields, but not in this proposal, to keep the changes
small and simple.

Currently only the liveblog model uses the `id` and `blockId` fields from frontend, and the frontend
`modelBodyBlocks` are only used for forwarding to dotcom rendering, so the code in frontend
will only change minimally.

To ensure no existing code is broken by the refactor, we will follow these steps:
- Update the Frontend `BodyBlock` to use the new `elements` field.
- Update the Frontend test code.
- Update the Frontend `LiveBlog.blocks` field to get `elements`.
- Update dotcom rendering to use the new `elements` field instead of `content` and match the Frontend 
model (renaming `content` to `elements`).
- Update dotcom rendering to use block id instead of block number.
- Update the dotcom rendering `LiveBlogBodyBlock` to accept block id.

## Decision: * The wrappers we create should replace the Nunjucks components for all non MDTP team use cases. 
* To make them easy to discover and consistent we should
  * mirror the original Govuk/HMRC Nunjucks components
  * use the same noun + modifier naming scheme.

For example,
* we are replacing the Nunjucks hmrcHeader with a MDTP wrapper of type Header, named GovukHmrcHeader
* we are replacing the Govuk Nunjucks pagination with a MDTP wrapper of type Pagination, named GovukPagination.

### Consistency of Names

As MDTP component wrappers will replace the ported Nunjucks components for all non MDTP team use cases, 
we should be consistent and only provide the MDTP wrappers and not the ported Nunjucks component implementations in 
the library. 

This, however, would be a breaking change and require 100s of repositories to rewrite calls using Nunjucks components to
use the new wrappers. This approach goes against the MDTP principle of `making small changes, frequently`.

Instead,
* for now, ported Nunjucks components that are being wrapped and replaced by the new MDTP component helpers
  * will be prefixed with **LegacyGovuk** or **LegacyHmrc**
  * to indicate they are legacy
  * to avoid clashing with the new MDTP component wrappers
  * and to make them easy to search for, discover and replace.
* Any Govuk Nunjucks components ported that do not have their own MDTP wrappers will
  * be kept as **Govuk***
  * to follow the same naming convention for new components
  * and to avoid breaking existing users of such components that have not had new wrappers created.

For example
* GovukHeader becomes LegacyGovukHeader (new wrapper will be GovukHeader)
* HmrcHeader becomes LegacyHmrcHeader (new wrapper will be GovukHmrcHeader)
* GovukDateInput remains GovukDateInput as no new wrapper has been created as yet
* GovukSelect remains GovukSelect as no new wrapper has been created as yet.

In future releases we will remove all Legacy* Nunjucks components from the library and rename all remaining 
Nunjucks components with a Legacy* prefix if a new wrapper is implemented for them.

### Consistency of APIs

* Wrapper function parameters will
  * include parameters to facilitate MDTP wiring as discussed above
  * default to MDTP platform best practice values where possible e.g. for `serviceName` in GovukHeader
  * include an additional `requestHeader` or `request` parameter to facilitate MDTP wiring

```scala
object GovukHeader {

  def apply(
    serviceName: Option[Text],
    serviceUrl: Option[String],
    containerClasses: String = "",
    containerId: String = "",
    navigation: Seq[GovukHeaderNavigation],
    assetsUrl: Option[String] = Some(AppConfig.assetsPrefix),
    nonce: Option[String] = None
  )(implicit rh: RequestHeader, messages: Messages): Html =
    Html(render(govukHeader(
      serviceName = serviceName,
      serviceUrl = serviceUrl,
      containerClasses = containerClasses,
      containerId = containerId,
      navigation = GovukHeaderNavigation.toNunjucks(navigation),
      assetsUrl = assetsUrl,
      language = Some(messages.lang.code)
    ).toString, nonce))
}
```

* MDTP wrappers will provide common object builders to simplify creation of required Nunjucks objects e.g.
  * GovukDateInput can be constructed with `GovukDateInput(date = Option(Date.today))` instead of
    `GovukDateInput(date = Some(Date(year = 2021, month = 1, day = 1)))`
  * GovukErrorSummary can be constructed with `GovukErrorSummary.build(title = "test", body = "test")`
    instead of `GovukErrorSummary(title = Some(Text("test")), errorList = Some(Seq(ErrorSummary(text = Some(Text("test"))))))`
  * GovukHeader can be constructed with `GovukHeader(serviceName = Option(Text("test")), ...) ` instead of
    `GovukHeader(serviceName = Some(Text("test")), ...) `

## Decision: I have decided that Cognito User Pools and Federated Identities are the right solution for authentication and identity management. Cognito User Pools provide a place to register new users in a database managed by AWS, while Federated Identities provide a mechanism for authenticating through an identity provider and acquiring temporary credentials to speak to other AWS services. Cognito does a few other things, but this is the minimum needed to acquire a working identity pool.

In particular, the approach I will implement has the following steps, mostly following [this tutorial][identity]:

- Create a User Pool that holds all the registered app users. Set it to work with a federated identity provider (GitHub, Google, etc.).
- Create an Identity Pool that holds the various identity providers.
- Create an "Authenticated User Role" in IAM. This role defines which AWS resources authenticated users can access, but in this implementation, Cognito will create it for me by default.
- Integrate the User Pool into Identity Pool to allow User Pool users to authenticate and get credentials.
- Test it with a CLI (curl) and get the token.
- Integrate this process with the client.

To make things easy, I'm just going to integrate Cognito directly into the existing project. I've heard some talk that it's better to manage Cognito from its own CloudFormation template that's distinct from the backend. The tutorials that I'm reading suggest putting it into the backend's serverless file so I'm doing that.

## Decision: We are looking for a library to ease tracing development for user code. We reviewed OpenTelemetry for this purpose as it is merging OpenTracing and OpenCensus into a single project. The project is getting more mature and stable now. We don't need to support all the APIs since users could write their own custom instrumentation. The core APIs for the libraries to support tracing are TraceProvider, Tracer, Span, and Context.

We decided to use OpenTelemetry library to support distributed tracing. We are also planning to add support for OpenTelemetry SDK instead of having a separate TraceProvider APIs. This will make it easy to align to OpenTelemetry standard.

### OpenTelemetry Go Library

OpenTelemetry is supported for gRPC, and it supports distributed trace context header format. However, it still lacks some features like:

- [No official API for tracing HTTP](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go/issues/192)
- [Add `SpanContextFromJSON` and `SpanContextToJSON` functions](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go/issues/216)
- Need to manually import header to gRPC metadata

### Use OpenTelemetry and some additional custom code

We create the APIs on the top of OpenTelemetry to hide the implementation details and make it easy to get started to add OpenTelemetry APIs and features after the project gets more stable.

**User code APIs**

- To use existing SpanContext to create child Span
```
traceID := tracing.TraceID(r) // r is *http.Request or gRPC metadata
spanContext := tracing.SpanContextFromID(traceID)
spanName := tracing.SpanNameFromRequest(r)
span := tracing.StartSpanFromContext(spanContext, spanName, nil, nil)
defer span.End()
```

- To create root Span
```
span := tracing.StartSpan("root span", nil, nil, nil)
defer span.End()
```

- To inject span context to HTTP header
```
client := &http.Client{}
req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", url, nil)
req.Header.Set(tracing.DistributedTraceContextHeader, span.SpanContextToID())
client.Do(req)
```

- To inject span context to gRPC metadata
```
conn, err := grpc.Dial(address, grpc.WithInsecure())
md := metadata.New(map[string]string{tracing.DistributedTraceContextHeader: span.SpanContextToID()})
ctx := metadata.NewOutgoingContext(context.Background(), md)
client := pb.NewMyServiceClient(conn)
response, err := client.MyMethod(ctx, &pb.HelloRequest{SayHello: "hello"})
```

### Future Work

- Change API signature: to pass existing context to StartSpan API, instead of passing SpanContext
```
StartSpanFromContext(r.Context(), spanName)
StartSpanFromContext(context.Background(), rootSpanName)
```

## Decision: ======
All container images should use the smallest base image possible, with the smallest behavior diff between local dev (WSL2) and container environments.

The team has evaluated several approaches, including:
* Custom `alpine:3.15` (our current image, with additional packages installed such as `ca-certificates`)
* `mcr.microsoft.com/cbl-mariner/base/core`
* `ubuntu:focal`

The team found that each option had their own unique sets of trade-offs:
* All 3 options failed on different unit tests, indicating behavioral differences
* `ubuntu:focal` had the highest overall usage in the ecosystem
* CBL-Mariner is the least used ecosystem, but has the advantage of having the most recent packages. It is also the smallest of the options tested.

The following table summarizes a few of the results from the evaluation:

| Image            | Install size (MB)  | Base `tar.gz` size (MB) |
|------------------|--------------------|-------------------------|
| `ubuntu:focal`   | 72.84              | 29.56                   |
| `cbl-mariner:2`  | 44.59              | 16.92                   |
| `alpine:3.15`    | 5.86               | 2.76                    |
| *Custom alpine*  | 27.2               | 9.5                     |

We also found the following issues when trying to run our unit tests in container images built from these bases:
* `ubuntu:focal`: fails to compile unit tests, likely due to older version of `openssl`
* `cbl-mariner:2`: fails with core dumps in unit tests; after extensive debugging it is unclear why the failures are occurring
* `alpine:3.15`: fails due to missing `libc`; after installing the `gcompat` package, the tests pass for the `aws-crt-go` repo. The `aws-iot-device-sdk-cpp-v2` tests failed due to a missing `libc++` library. Installing the `clang-dev` package solved the problem, and all the tests passed.

## Decision: Code will be organized to be compatible with:
- `mypy`:
  - `mypy` does not support relative imports within an empty module. If a `__init__.py` file exists in a directory, `mypy` assumes that directory to be a package. [relevant discussion](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/52174304/is-import-mpy-supported-by-mypy)
  - `mypy` requires absolute imports from the base directory
- `pytest`:
  - `pytest` does not support absolute imports unless a parent directory is added to the system path. [relevant discussion](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/10253457/is-there-a-way-to-import-parent-modules-with-pytest)
  - `pytest` supports relative imports within a module
- `sphinx-autodoc-typehints`
  - `sphinx-autodoc-typehints` requires the full path to an object for it to hyperlink correctly, e.g. `cypage.types.attribute.SubAttribute`

A compromise for these requirements was found using the following file structure for the `attribute.py` module within the `cypage.types` package:
- `cypage/types/__init__.py`:

```
__all__ = ["attribute", ...]
from cypage.types import attribute
...
```

- `cypage/types/attribute.py`:

```
from __future__ import annotations
import sys
if sys.version_info >= (3, 8):
    from typing import Literal
    from typing import Protocol
    from typing import runtime_checkable
else:
    from typing import Type
    from typing import overload
    import typing_extensions

    class Protocol(typing_extensions.Protocol):
        ...

    def overload(func):
        return func

    def runtime_checkable(cls):
        return cls

    class _Literal(Type[object]):  # pylint: disable=protected-access,inherit-non-class
        def __getitem__(self, items):
            return typing_extensions.Literal[items]

    Literal = _Literal()
```

### Type annotation usage
- When referring to another type:
  - If the other type is defined in the same file, use the bare name, e.g. `SubAttribute`
  - If the other type is defined in another file in the same package (e.g. the other type is `AttributeType` and the current type is defined in `cypage/types/attribute.py`), use the full import path from the package root, e.g. `types.attribute.AttributeType`
  - If the other type is defined in another package, use the full import path from the module root, e.g. `cypage.types.attribute.AttributeType`

An example of this usage can be seen in the following excerpt of `SubAttribute` from the `cypage.types.attribute.py` module:

```
@runtime_checkable
class SubAttribute(Protocol):  # pylint: disable=too-few-public-methods
    @property
    def name(self) -> Literal["column.names"]:  # pylint: disable=too-many-branches,too-many-statements
        ...

    @overload
    @classmethod
    def get_attribute(cls, attribute_type: Literal[types.attribute.AttributeType.SUBNETWORKS]) -> "SubAttribute":  # pylint: disable=line-too-long
        ...

    @classmethod
    def get_attribute(cls, attribute_type: types.attribute.AttributeType) -> "SubAttribute":  # pylint: disable=line-too-long
        if attribute_type == types.attribute.AttributeType.SUBNETWORKS:
            return SubNetworkAttribute()
        raise ValueError(f"{attribute_type} is not a valid SubAttribute")
```

## Decision: The **genome ID** [^3] and **object type** are combined using the `:` character  
These are combined with the **object ID** using the `#` character  
All `#` and `:` characters are URI encoded

The following syntax will therefore be adopted to refer to an Ensembl object:

    <genome_id>:<object_type>#<object_id>

### Examples:
- A gene, ENSG00000139618, from the Human GRCh38 genome (genome_id `homo_sapiens_GCA_000001405_14`):  
    `homo_sapiens_GCA_000001405_14:gene#ENSG00000139618`  
- A region/slice/location, 13:32315474-32400266, from the Human GRCh38 genome (genome_id `homo_sapiens_GCA_000001405_14`):  
    `homo_sapiens_GCA_000001405_14:region#13%3A32315474-32400266`  

### Decomposing an Ensembl object ID string  
The following regexp can be used for decomposition:  
`^(?<genome_id>[^:]+):(?<object_type>[^#]+)#(?<object_id>.+)$`

For example:  
```js  
const ensemblObjectId = 'homo_sapiens_GCA_000001405_14:region#13%3A32315474-32400266';

const match = ensemblObjectId.match(/^(?<genome_id>[^:]+):(?<object_type>[^#]+)#(?<object_id>.+)$/);  

const { genome_id, object_type, object_id } = match.groups;  

console.log('genome_id', genome_id); // homo_sapiens_GCA_000001405_14
console.log('object_type', object_type); // region
console.log('object_id', decodeURIComponent(object_id)); // 13:32315474-32400266
```

---  
[^3]: For the time being we will use the `assembly.assembly_accession` to refer to the genome ID, however there is an initiative to create a separate Ensembl genome ID which will need to be adopted when it becomes available.

## Decision: We are going to adopt a new pattern for how to export symbols in our packages.
Instead of allowing arbitrary re-exports, we will introduce a `src/index.ts`
root package entry point that will control all exports from the package. This
entrypoint will only allow re-exports from `src/api.ts` and `src/components/`,
which makes it easy to follow all package exports by simply checking the
contents of `src/index.ts`. All of these re-exports from `src/api.ts` and
`src/components` must be explicit re-exports (ie no `export *`), as the export
star operator tends to hide the actual public API for users of the module.

The re-exports within `src/api.ts` and `src/components` are less restricted.
For convenience it is allowed to use `export * from ...` to re-export an
entire directory in one line, but it is also allowed to use explicit named
re-exports. `src/api.ts` and `src/components` themselves can also re-export
exports from each other or other packages.

In summary:

```
+------------+     +-------------------+     +---------------------+
|src/index.ts| <-- |src/api.ts         |     |src/components/...   |
|            |     |                   |<----|src/components/index.ts|
|export *    |     |                   |     |                     |
|from api.ts |     |                   |     |                     |
|            |     |                   |<--------------------------+
|export *    |     |                   |
|from        |     |                   |
|components/ |     |                   |
|            |     |                   |
+------------+     +-------------------+
```

Note: The `src/index.ts` file must always be present, and must not import any
non-public module. Also, the `src/api.ts` file must always be present.

When this is merged, it will not be enforced by any CI job or test. Instead
it should be something that we keep in mind when opening PRs and doing reviews.

## Decision: ### Background

We had implemented a `ds-dropdown-menu` with default click listener on each menu item to close itself on click.

```javascript
/* ds-dropdown-menu/index.js */
this.listeners.click = event => this.close()
```

This made it very easy to use the menu and required little effort for a common use-case.

Later, we decided to add the option to set event handlers on individual menu items by extending the `ds-dropdown-menu` component.
Because menu item handlers were now a property of the menu, and not the menu items, the event bubbled up to the menu, and both listeners would be triggered causing unexpected behavior.


### What happens?

In our example:

1. `ds-dropdown-menu` was set to close on every click.
2. We then added `onClick` option property to each menu item, to do other things, like triggering a search.

Expected: click menu item > trigger a search.
Actual: click menu item > close menu and trigger a search.


### Other use cases

Adding extra functionality or styles as the default when creating web components:

1. Changing an icon to be outlined version on click
2. Making an item visible, hidden or disabled on click or focus


### Proposal

We've decided to avoid this practice and not to add any default click/focus/etc listeners directly into our web components, unless they are specific to this web component (i.e. click to expand `ds-collapse`) and won't conflict with consumer's future customization.

We will focus on providing component's API to:
1. set click/focus listeners
2. set other attributes, like `aria-label`, `disabled`, `visible`
3. programmatically trigger changes

Here is how to solve our `ds-dropdown-menu` use-case:
https://github.com/designsystem/web-components/blob/e7b919d3ee3844f2b96e488182b8a78018e6ec29/components/ds-dropdown-menu/stories/index.stories.js#L57

## Decision: - **Incubation:** This describes features currently in early stages of development.
  The James community has no current plans to complete those.
  They are delivered to external users in the hope that it will help us gather feedbacks and
  gauge community interest around it to help prioritizing.
- **Experimental:** This describes features for which James has a current plans to get to stable state.
  These can be features in early stages of development or almost completed features needing community
  testing. Experimental modules and features can and most likely will change without backward-compatibility
  guarantees. They might also break with new James release. If you wish to use experimental
  features you should subscribe to the developer mailing list and watch James GitHub repository to
  keep up-to-date with changes related to it. You will have to adapt your code accordingly.
- **Testing:** This describes artifacts we plan to deprecate and delete in short term and for which
  we want to get community feedback. Their status might evolve quickly to either Deprecated or Experimental
  depending on community feedback. Those also have no guarantee around backward-compatibility. If you wish
  to use testing features you should subscribe to the developer mailing list and watch James GitHub
  repository to keep up-to-date with changes related to it. You will have to adapt your code accordingly.
- **Stable:** This describes James artifacts and features currently in maintenance mode with a strong
  commitment to backward-compatibility. Stable modules or features are assumed to not be deleted unless
  they are explicitly announced as deprecated or testing (a new ADR must be written and approved in the
  meantime). Stable modules and features will always be adapted in order to support recent technologies.
  If the changes needed to achieve this break backward-compatibility, the community will explicitly deprecate the feature
  and introduce the new one as a replacement feature with an experimental status to keep providing support
  for past versions.
  Stable artifacts and features can and most likely will evolve as long as they provide backward-compatibility.
  Those changes might include addition of new feature.

The status for each artifacts will be defined in a README file. Each of the feature within an artifact
will be clearly identified by a README in the sub-folder/README.

When new artifacts and features are designed and delivered to users they should be considered at Incubation

## Decision: ### We will use SHA256 as our primary hash function, but continue to support the use of
RIPEMD160 in its previous roles for the time being.

The cryptographic community has settled on SHA256 as the standard algorithm, with optimized support in hardware.

### We will use the same Merkle tree construction.
However, it should be possible to use it with any hash function that meets the interface, so that we may migrate
off of SHA256 in the future if a stronger algorithm is discovered (eg. [STARKWare's FRI](https://medium.com/starkware/a-look-under-the-hood-of-fri-d09a5666f7f4)).

### Addresses will continue to be computed using the RipEMD160 of the amino encoding of the public key.
While we considered updating the algorithm to SHA256, it was determined that the benefits (performance, more secure, modern)
were outweighed by the cost of changing addresses after they have been in use for some time.
It's possible that this could change in the future, if a strong security vulnerability is discovered.

### We will update the P2P connection to use ChaCha20+Poly1305 and Blake2s-256 for the encryption and hashing.
There are a number of libraries we can use to implement this, so we'll review those in future pull requests.

We also considered replacing the P2P implementation with a solution like [WireGuard](https://www.wireguard.com),
which is currently the "gold standard" for VPNs. While it's probably the most secure, it also comes with a lot of
dependencies which would greatly increase the difficulty in the implementation.

## Decision: Do not introduce stateful components to Octagon.  Wherever possible, all Octagon components should be functional / presentational.

**Important**: This does not mean _no_ state is allowed.  For instance, we want to allow for dynamic width of tables.  This cannot easily be determined by props.

Instead, we have decided to define:

- **State** (embedded) as a component's rendering & behavior being _defined by_ internal state.
- **Internal** as state that may live _inside_ a component, but does not define behavior/rendering.
  Example: The table component above would use local state to track column widths, but this is an internal rendering detail & the table would render exactly the same whether local state was used to track these details, or not.  The table's _behavior_ and _rendering_ is defined entirely via props.
- Internal state could always be replaced by props, with no change to the rendering & behavior.  Instead, internal state would be replaced by props if the consuming application wishes to provide this data externally, and control it.

The component being rendered & behavior will always be definied by props and not state.  We will never make a component's rendering & behavior dependent on local state.

## Decision: We've agreed that as a rule of thumb, utility classes are created when they're:
- Useful: Are they something we use repeatedly?
- Unopinionated: Can they be used in any application to do the same thing? (this makes them good candidates for sharing and re-use)
- Small: Can you express what the class does in the smallest possible statement?
  - E.g. `display--none` says what it does without specifying a breakpoint, container, or context.
  - E.g. `padding-bottom--20` vs `padding-bottom--20-on-mobile` (more specific context)
  - E.g. `grid` vs `grid-columns-5` (more specific context)

When we have a more complex usecase that requires a mixture of utility classes, we add component styles. Components
should be created to fulfil a specific need that isn't shared across different contexts.

A good sign a utility class is needed, is where we find ourselves with lots of components that include the same utility
classes.

This is an iterative process. It's perfectly fine to start with a component and later refactor it to use utility
classes, as it becomes clearer what can be moved to utilities.

## Decision: To increase the number of supported metadata values and remain within the limit
placed by Stripe we will implement the following solutions:

* Replace Metadata Values with References to an external data store.
* Utilize the [Stripe Descriptions API][stripe-descriptions] in place of metadata
  where the functionality can be replaced with descriptions.
* We may also explore using [JSON encoding](https://stripe.com/docs/api/metadata#metadata_object-description) 
  to store multiple metadata fields within one metadata value (which still counts
  as a single metadata value).

### Reference to an external data store

Where it makes sense and is possible we will reference an external source of
metadata instead of embedding the metadata value within a Stripe metadata key.
By storing our own version of the metadata we have full control over the amount
of data we store and are only limited by our own storage. The external
data store that we have decided to use is a [Static S3 Website][static-s3]. We have
selected a Static S3 Website as our data store as it is a highly reliable
solution, requires no ongoing maintenance and has an extremely low cost.

## Decision: This ADR defines a new micro-service, 'spreadsheet_validator' to address this
problem. It will be implemented in [Python](https://www.python.org/) utilizing
the [Pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/) library. In terms of design, it would
be easiest to implement and test each spreadsheet validator as a new function
that is then mapped to an HTTP call with the name of the corresponding
spreadsheet. When a spreadsheet is to be validated, the user would POST that
spreadsheet to an endpoint, with the name of the spreadsheet, and get a JSON
response with a PASS/FAIL and any validation issues. It could also provide some
sort of message, whether or not the spreadsheet passed validation or not. The
service will have three main sections: spreadsheet validation, error handling,
and RESTful API.

### Spreadsheet Validation

This section provides the logic that is utilized when an HTTP POST request is
submitted with the spreadsheet. Each new spreadsheet to be validated will have
its own function. The function's main components will be:

* Column Validation
* Header Row Validation
* Cell Validation (each row and cell individually)
* Return a validation result

An example for `metadata.csv` can be found [here](examples/metadata.md).

#### Column Validation

Column validation verifies that the number of expected columns matches what is
in the spreadsheet.

#### Header Row Validation

Each spreadsheet has an expected header row. Header row validation will check
that the column names are present and in the expected order. If there is a need
to not follow the expected order, an entry will be added to the spreadsheet and
validator in order to address this.

#### Cell Validation

Cell validation is at the core of the service. All cells in all rows are passed
through a function to validate the cells. Validation checks would include:

* Expected date/time format
* Integer format (if appropriate)
* Any value in a list of allowed values
* URL format

Additional validation checks will be added as needed.

#### Validation Result

Validation result would simply indicate if a PASS/FAIL occurred. A FAIL will
then include any of the issues found during validation.

#### Required Columns for Validation

In order to avoid validating columns that are of less concern to the user
(though all columns will be validated), a configuration option will be provided
to select columns that must be present in order to pass validation. This will
be utilized with the column validation check described above.

### Error Handling

The service will utilize [Flask's
logging](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/1.1.x/logging/) and Python's
[`logging`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html) modules. It will
have a general catch all if the POST to the web service has an
unsupported spreadsheet. Errors during spreadsheet validation will be collected
into a list and returned to the user in a JSON format. The service will return
200 on all error messages.

### RESTful API

The service will implement a RESTful API and the only supported method will be
HTTP POST.

`http://spreadsheetvalidator.org/validate/<spreadsheet_type>/` where
`<spreadsheet_type>` can be a specific type of spreadsheet (e.g. metadata). The
HTTP POST should contain the spreadsheet contents, not the path.

Here is an example, assuming the `metadata.csv` was found under
`path/to/spreadsheet_directory/`:

```
curl -X POST \
  http://spreadsheetvalidator.org/validate/metadata \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet' \
  --data-binary "@path/to/spreadsheet_directory/metadata.xlsx"
```

A return with a PASS:

```json
{
    "validation": "pass"
}
```

A return with a FAIL:

```json
{
    "errors": [
        "Column mismatch at header: expected 'identifier_type', got 'description_level'",
        "Missing required column 'identifier_type'",
        "Column mismatch at header: expected 'object_type', got 'identifier'",
        "Missing required column 'object_type'",

## Decision: * The ordering system will be updated with actual data whenever possible, thus minimizing the window of concurrency
* No changes will be applied to the system whenever the smart fridge system is offline

### The ordering system will be updated with actual data whenever possible, thus minimizing the window of concurrency

Whenever changes occur on the smart fridge (e.g. food delivery), the ordering systems needs to be updated with actual data (e.g. food types and amount). To avoid concurrency problems, the smart fridge system is updated by the following procedure:

1. Update the ordering systems with actual data (food types and amount) from the smart fridge system
2. The ordering systems then responds with the total amount of available funds for pre-paid meals
3. Update the smart fridge system with actual data (food types and amount) from the ordering system

![Inventory data flow](adr-0005-image-01.png "Smart fridge inventory data flow")

### No changes will be applied to the system whenever the smart fridge system is offline

![Online and offline ordering](adr-0005-image-02.png "Online and offline ordering")

The smart fridge system informs the ordering systems when it is offline.

Whenever the ordering systems detects that the smart fridge is offline, no changes will be applied to the ordering systems inventory.

The smart fridge systems will take care of pre-paid meals and cash purchases in offline mode.

## Decision: The decision is that we will not be creating a decorator or a separate class. We will use two separate functions to create the required DAG/table: `get_model_inputs` and `get_model_outputs`. Each function will take the `ast.Node` as input and return the model input/output as a dictionary.

To deal with the problem of input and output of a function sharing a common argument we will change the way the inputs/outputs are derived.

For the inputs a distinction between "mandatory" and "optional" inputs will be made. The mandatory inputs will be defined as those that must be included to run a DAG/table. All other inputs will be assumed to be optional and the user will have to decide which ones they want to include and then manually merge them together into the dictionary produced by `get_model_inputs`.

The `outputs` for a function will be taken from the returned values in `return` statement(s) and these will be appended to a list. This means that if you return three values and store them to three variables `a,b,c` these will be added as `{'outputs': ['a', 'b', 'c']}`.

### `get_model_inputs`
`get_model_inputs` is given an `ast.Node` object (e.g the `redshift_gamma` function from above). `ast` can be used to convert the function into a list of tuples like this:
```python
ast.get_arg(redshift_gamma) -> [('shape', None), ('scale', None), ('size', None)]
```
`get_model_inputs` will then convert this list of arguments into a dictionary of input arguments that are needed to produce a DAG/table.

The keys in the dictionary will be the argument names that are inputs to the `redshift_gamma` function (i.e `shape`, `scale`, `size`).

The values in the dictionary will contain the default values for the function and also the source of the parameter (i.e parameter, filename, function name, etc.). The value will also include the docstrings describing the argument. This could be derived from the Sphinx docstrings of the function or it would be left to the user to manually include these in the YAML file

### `get_model_outputs`
`get_model_outputs` will be used to determine what columns the `redshift_gamma` function produces when run. The returned value for `get_model_inputs` could be stored for use in other simulations that require the results of `redshift_gamma`.

`get_model_outputs` is given an `ast.Node` object. `ast` can be used to produce the list of values returned from the function like this:
```python
ast.get_returned_values(redshift_gamma) -> ['redshift']
```
`get_model_inputs` will then convert this list of values into a list of output arguments. In this case `redshift` will be appended to the list and the final result will be `{'outputs':['redshift']}`

### Model file
A YAML file will still be used to create the DAG. All information required to create the input dictionary will be taken from the YAML file and all model outputs will be read as a list.

A draft YAML file can be found in a separate `Model` directory and all work should be focused on making sure the Python `Model` functionality can read this file correctly.

## Decision: ### Directive

We need to provide cloud hosting for 2 categories of services:

1.  **Transactional services** with varying complexity and transaction volumes where the underlying platforms (hardware, software, data centres, etc.) are managed by the cloud provider. We need to be confident of the resilience and scalability of the platform. We need to retain full control over the application stack, data and user experience. Examples include the DigiTS service and future framework services. This type of hosting comes under PaaS (Platform as a service) or SaaS (Software as a service)

2.  **Data processing and analytics** where the underlying platforms are managed by the cloud provider. We need to be confident of the resilience and scalability of the platform and the integrity of the data. We need to retain full control over the application and the integrity of the data. This type of hosting comes under PaaS.

We have a requirement for our cloud hosting platform(s) to be reliable, secure, scalable and provide value for money. There are multiple platforms in the marketplace and the decision must be robust and auditable.

Having considered the 4 main options available to CCS:

*   Building our own service in AWS
*   Building our own service in Azure
*   Using Government-as-a-Platform PaaS/IaaS as provided by GDS (based on AWS)
*   Procuring a complete (SaaS) service via the Digital Marketplace 

We propose to adopt the following approach:

1.  **For Transactional services**, we will default to using GDS’s PaaS/IaaS managed service running on AWS. If it is not possible to use this service, perhaps due to limitations (eg for the Data Submission Service) we will build our own service on AWS.
1.  **For Data processing and analytics services** we will use Microsoft Azure, where the existing warehouse and reporting environment sits. The new Data Submission Service is likely to use this.
1.  We will continue to manage existing (and procure future) Software-as-a-service solutions from suppliers where appropriate.

This approach gives CCS the benefits of cloud hosting and a common platform approach, whilst leveraging the Government-as-a-platform initiative.

### Consequences

*   This approach is simple and easy to communicate
*   GDS have experience of running highly available services at scale
*   Cost effective – GDS leverage economies of scale in platform management, procurement and licensing
*   Using GDS PaaS/IaaS provides support for a range of programming languages and approaches
*   AWS is the most advanced cloud platform in the world, with new services and features available regularly
*   Azure is the closest cloud provider to AWS in terms of capability
*   Provides a degree of consistency across the hosting environment without forcing a 1 size fits all approach
*   Increases skills transferability amongst staff
*   Removes the need to make hosting decisions for future transactional services
*   Allows CMp frameworks to leverage the Digital Marketplace platform, if CMp choose to go down that route

## Decision: We will make use of DNS to give the operator flexibility to configure their system.

It is proposed we implement a Service Definition that is an intermediate step between the Task Definition and the state machine.

Example
```
{
    "Comment": "Start an EC2 instance",
    "ServiceDefinitionArn": "arn:aws:states:::services:start-ec2",
    "Parameters": {
      "ResourceName": "some-ec2-name"
    }
}
```

The ServiceDefinition in this example would look like
```
{
    "Comment": "Start an EC2 instance",
    "ResourceName": "start-ec2.internal.mdscloud.net",
    "TaskDefinition": {
      "Resource": "http://{{ Parameters.ResourceName }}"
      "ResultPath": "$",
      "TimeoutSeconds": 60
    }
}
```

Where the mdsCloud stack should generate DNS records for all services. TheseDNS entries would have the following form:

- **Type**: CNAME
- **Name**: ${service_name}.internal.mdscloud.net
- **Value**: ${IP_ADDRESS} or ${CNAME of service}

The ServiceDefinition will be specified via environment variables so the mdscloud stack does not need to know a priori about all the different possible service integrations.

Service definitions should allow for the following parameters:
 - Comments
 - Resource name (DNS name of service)
 - InputPath/OutputPath for the task
 - ResultPath
 - Task definition

The default task definition for this approach will be
```
{
    "Type": "Task",
    "Resource": "http://{{ Parameters.ResourceName }}",
    "ResultPath": "$",
    "TimeoutSeconds": 60
}
```

This way a simple service definition can be
```
{
    "Comment": "Start an EC2 instance",
    "ServiceDefinitionArn": "arn:aws:states:::services:start-ec2",
    "Parameters": {
      "ResourceName": "some-ec2-name"
    }
}
```

```
export "SERVICE_DEFINITIONS = [
  {
      "Comment": "Start an EC2 instance",
      "ResourceName": "start-ec2.internal.mdscloud.net"
      "ServiceDefinitionArn": "arn:aws:states:::services:start-ec2"
  },
  {
      "Comment": "Stop an EC2 instance",
      "ResourceName": "stop-ec2.internal.mdscloud.net"
      "ServiceDefinitionArn": "arn:aws:states:::services:stop-ec2"
  }
]"
```

## Decision: To achieve our goal and providing the label to developers, we decided to provide the label for every custom field via
a separate Store API route. This has the advantage, that we don't have to load it for every entity.
As the number of custom fields are often limited, we can cache the result of the labels via HTTP caching, as the labels
often do not change.
The label of a custom field can then be retrieved via a call to `store-api/custom-field-label`.
As we expect to have only a limited amount of translations available for the labels of the custom fields, we decided
to provide a map where the key is the locale of the translation and the value is the translated label.
This is necessary to save as much requests to the API as possible.
Another advantage is, that all necessary labels can be fetched with one call to the store api and the label can then
be applied in JavaScript where necessary.
With this map it is easy to filter the label by a specified locale.
For the case, that the custom field label has no translation in a specific locale, we provide a placeholder.
It can either be the name of the custom field or a static string that should represent the custom field.

### Store API route

```text
GET store-api/custom-field-label

{
  "apiAlias": "custom_field_label_response",
  "data": {
    "custom_field_1": {
      "de-DE": "Deutsch",
      "en-GB": "English"
    },
    "custom_field_2": {
      "de-DE": "Deutsch"
    }
  }
}
```

The route contains a map of all custom field labels.

The key is the name of the custom field and value is an array of custom field labels, where the locale is the key
and the translated label is the value.

## Decision: The general idea is to isolate features, bugs and chores branches from our `main` branch. This process would allow us to be able to follow each change independently from the others.

Each time a developer need to develop a feature, solve a bug or update the dependencies of the project, they must checkout a new branch (see below).

Then, a pull request should be opened, pointing to `main`. After receiving a positive review (ideally two reviewers), a test and the automated tasks were run, the PR can be accepted and merged. Once merged, the feature, bug or chore branch should be deleted.

##Decision: 1 and 2 require developers to change their workflow and will introduce friction
into the delivery process. 3 requires Github and therefore the delivery pipeline
to be up, and a failure in this process could prevent deployments. It's not
obvious how 3 provides any more protection against a malicious insider than our
existing process of at least one review on a PR, and checking PR merge.

The simplest solution that provides what we want, and doesn't add any developer
friction, is 1 above without the empty commits: when merging to master from
approved (by review) PR branches, we digitally sign the merge commit with an
organisation key controlled by a limited set of people. This allows the delivery
pipeline to verify the existence and validity of that signature using a trusted
public key, whilst allowing developers to continue to use their own git workflow
for their contributions and pull requests.

This should not be considered a silver bullet to preventing developers from
deploying malicious code, as that would require a much more thorough security
audit of the platform.

##Decision: We will use the TRUNCATE database reset strategy for the time being.

The primary reason to use transactions is for performance. But as noted above, we are not optimizing for speed at the moment. However, the time required for a database-transaction-wrapped test is less predictable than one that truncates.

Also, database transactions have a few drawbacks that make them undesirable given our testing situation:

* Transactions do not play well with concurrent operations.
* Tests cannot spawn new goroutines that themselves read from the same database transaction. While not in the test runner, the tests could themselves execute in a new goroutine and in that new goroutine open a transaction, and then pass that to the test under test.
* Not all databases support transactions equally well. (e.g. Postgres vs MongoDB)
* Not all SQL operations are atomic inside a transaction, like `CREATE TABLE`.

For these reasons, we have decided to stick to using a TRUNCATE approach to clearing the database between tests for now, but will likely swap to transactions once we have a deeper understanding of our future test concerns.

## Decision: We are building 2 Cloud Functions and a Python library in order to perform
this task.  The functions will use triggers and events to determine when to
run.

The first function will update the GCS object checksum in our MySQL
instance when objects are created or modified in GCS.  The function will
trigger on changes to GCS objects and retrieve the MD5 value in base64 encoding,
decode it into a hex string, and update the MySQL instance.

The second function will trigger on a time based schedule, periodically query
our MySQL instance for random entries, and generate events to perform checksum
validation on these entries.

The Python library will contain all of the core logic and dependencies to
decode the MD5 value and interact with the database.

  - Event Based Destruction, in this case it must be decided by domain experts when destruction must be done

## Decision: We've opted to redesign the process API in a very similar fashion to the

* The `ExecuteCommand()` function on the process handler has been replaced by
  `RouteCommandToInstance()`, an additional function on the `ProcessRoot`
  interface itself.

* The `RouteEventToInstance()` function on the process handler has been
  replaced by `RouteEventToInstance()`, an additional function on the

The following changes were also made, but are not direct analogs of changes to
the aggregate API:

* The `RouteEventToNewInstance()` function has been removed from the process
  handler because it is no longer necessary. Since the instance ID for a new

## Decision: The Modernisation Platform is a managed platform with a set of operational responsibilities to maintain the health and operations of the platform. The platform is continuously monitored and deployed and therefore the security aspects of the network are considered and deployed by the modernisation platform team.

The platform is designed with network security and operational resilience in mind, we therefore include the following security features that are managed by the modernisation platform team and cannot be changed by tenants:

* Secure networking topology to ensure that it has private networks for its services.
* Firewalls and networks security groups are included to restrict network traffic between tenants (tenant to tenant) and also from the Internet to any part of the tenant infrastructure.
* DDoS protection at the network edge to help protect tenant applications and services from volumetric and protocol layer attacks.
* TLS version and cipher suite version restrictions for all network services

We expect tenants to implement their own network security by designing, testing and deploying application specific network security controls as part of their CI/CD processes.

A number of network security and operational resilience features have been built in to the platform with a number of specific decisions having been made and these are as follows:

## Decision: We are going to use Hexagonal Architecture as component architecture pattern.
Hexagonal architecture, aka ports and adapters pattern, was invented by A. Cockburn
to achieve a loose coupling between application layer concerns (business and presentation logic).
According to original idea from A. Cockburn, this pattern can be applied to either monoliths or
microservices, although he recommends hexagonal architecture and event-driven architecture
together for monolith-first applications.

The key aspects and benefits of using hexagonal architecture are:
* native support for application layer concerns separation
* loosely coupled application core from the surrounding technical concerns like UI and persistence layers
* native separation for presentation layer from the business logic layer
* domain-centric design approach, based on Domain-Driven Design (DDD) principles like ubiquitous language
  and bounded context
* enables easier porting to different platforms or technologies by just changing a specific adapter

### Chosen Option: hexagonal architecture

## Decision: Vi har valgt å kjøre med 2 brancher for kildekoden. Dette er en branch for hver av miljøene vi kjører applikasjonen i, preprod og prod. Når en Pull Request blir merget til preprod-branchen, deployes applikasjonen til preprod-miljøet. Fra preprod-branchen merger vi til prod-branchen, noe som deployer applikasjonen til produksjon. For å minimere sjansen for konflikter ved merging av preprod til prod, er det en beskyttet branch (https://docs.github.com/en/github/administering-a-repository/configuring-protected-branches), som tvinger oss til å rebase all historikk til preprod-branchen mot prod.

**Prod-branchen** holder koden som er i produksjon.
**Preprod-branchen** holder all funksjonalitet som er klar, men som enda ikke er i produksjon. Det er også denne som brukes til testing i testmiljøet.
**Alle featurebrancher og PR'er skal være mot Preprod**

**Rebase fra prod til preprod-branch**

Hvis Prod-branchen har blitt merget mot preprod fra en featurebranch må følgende gjøres:

```
git checkout preprod
git pull origin preprod
git rebase prod
```

Nå har preprod fått all historikken til prod lagt på preprod.

```
git checkout prod
git merge preprod
```

Prod-branchen får da historikken til preprod. Du kan trygt pushe og deploye til produksjon.

## Decision: - **Pull Request**: A set of changes to be reviewed by other people in the team before being delivered.

  We want PR to be as small as possible and short-lived as much as possible, as the benefits of using PR decrease drastically the longer they are open.

  As a rule of thumb, an open PR older than **one hour** should be delivered. If more time is needed, you might need to split it in multiple PRs and/or get help from another team member.

  This also means that the development workflow should be:

  1. Create a pull request to share the WIP immediately.
  1. Continue development by pushing new changes to the PR branch and asking other team members for feedback.
  1. Once the changes are considered acceptable by both the author and other people in the team, merge and deliver.

  PR should have a concise title that clearly communicates the change, as well as a description that explains the change in more detail if needed.

  References to issues, stories or any other external resource, should also be added.

  When approving the PR, please add a description that explains the rational behind the approval and any concern you might still have but you're willing to work on with the PR author.

  When rejecting, please add a description that explains why you're rejecting the PR.

  You can find an example of how a PR should look like [here](https://github.com/alphagov/cpm/pull/29/files).

## Decision: Chosen Option: "Creating a new ASG for every LC" because it is the most terraform friendly. This approach requires that there is a way to trigger the recreation of the ASG. To address this the approach uses a version to allow forcing a recreation of an ASG. The LC version is set with the format `YYYY-MM-DD.<lc-version>` so that all ASGs will be recreated on the new year's first terraform run.

Example use:

```hcl
module "production_puppetserver" {
  source           = "./node_group"
  instance_ami     = "${var.ami}"
  instance_type    = "${var.production_puppetserver_type}"
  instance_size    = 1
  instance_role    = "puppetserver"
  instance_ami_filter_name = "ami-01d7e265c0ec62372"
  region           = "${var.region}"
  subnet_id        = "${var.public_subnet_id}"
  lc_version       = "2017-06-21.1" # A version tag to help force ASG recreation

  user_data_path   = "./puppetmaster/user-data.sh"

  extra_security_group_ids = [
    "${module.base_infra.puppetserver_security_group_id}",
    "${module.base_infra.bastion_ssh_security_group_id}",
    "${module.base_infra.puppetdb_security_group_id}",
  ]
}
```

The node group has also been refactored to allow a simpler setup for the ASG to manage instances that are not configured by Puppet. This requires adding a second LC configuration named `legacy_lc_version` and is intended to be used with the new ASG version. See the `admin_ssh` module for an example.

Consider the impact a debug statement has on the users of your software.
If `Log.debug` is called frequently enough then:

## Decision: There is a strong feeling that people would prefer a single-package approach. While there are a number of downsides to a single-package approach, those downsides are mitigated for users by a tool chain that includes semantic-release, a bundled JS approach that includes aggressive tree-shaking, a component version numbering and package versioning strategy, and the fact that we can always iterate on the package versioning strategy (from single-package to many-packages) at a later date, whereas starting with a many-package approach would make a conversion to single-package much more challenging due to the difficulties inherent in bundling multiple packages into a single one.

### Component versioning approach

- All components start with version `1.0.0`
- The top-level package version is bumped according to what version of which components it contains
- All changes to components that are published to NPM require a version bump to the top-level package
- Major breaking changes to components would trigger a breaking (major) release of the top-level package
- Major breaking changes that aren't API changes (e.g., HTML or CSS breaking changes, breaking behavior changes) require a new version of the component that can be pulled in as a variant via props (similar to how some bootstrap components allow for a variant prop)
- Users are allowed to set the package version range to whatever they want for their app, but are encouraged to set a "caret" range (e.g. `^1.0.0`) so that their app will automatically use the latest component versions that are API-compatible with what they are already using.
